{"claims":[{"id":"c1","text":"Alpha (8–12 Hz) band-stop removal changes SAE latent firing much more than a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham notch in every setting. This raw signature looks like evidence for alpha features.","methods":["TopK SAEs (k=32) trained on frozen CBraMod, REVE and DINOv3 activations at early, middle and late depth on BCI, MA and Speech: 27 settings","Paired clean vs perturbed trials with a 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop; alpha vs width-matched 30–34 Hz sham","Metrics: |Δf_j|, active-set Jaccard, sparse-code cosine"],"results":["Raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio 7.33 (95% CI [6.18, 8.68]), >1 in 27/27 settings","Per-backbone raw ratios: CBraMod 7.4, REVE 8.9, DINOv3 5.1","Alpha lowers code overlap in all 27 settings","Alpha is the max-|Δf| and min-Jaccard band in only 15/27 settings of the six-band sweep (a plurality, not a rule)","Raw code-overlap ratio 2.77"],"conditions":["Frozen backbones and frozen SAEs","Fixed splits; data at 200 Hz","CIs bootstrapped over settings, not latents"]},{"id":"c2","text":"The raw alpha signature is largely an artifact of input distortion. EEG power falls as 1/f, so the alpha notch deletes far more signal than the sham, and the advantage collapses once responses are normalized by how much each notch removes.","methods":["Divide the SAE response by time-domain distortion ||x−x̃||2/||x||2","Divide the SAE response by the fraction of spectral energy removed"],"results":["Removed-energy ratios (alpha/sham): 57.2 (BCI), 34.6 (MA), 11.8 (Speech)","Time-normalized ratio 1.32 [1.12, 1.55], >1 in 17/27 settings","Spectral-normalized ratio 0.28 [0.22, 0.36], >1 in 0/27 settings","Code-overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then 0.51 and 0.11 after normalization"],"conditions":["The two normalizations bracket the confound rather than settle it","The removed-energy denominator varies almost fivefold across datasets","A band-stop cannot isolate a biological oscillator"]},{"id":"c3","text":"Alpha selectivity does not identify latents that matter to a linear task readout.","methods":["Selectivity s_{j,b} = |Δf_{j,b}| minus the mean |Δf| over the other five bands","Specialist-like latent: top quartile of alpha selectivity and at or below median channel-dropout fragility","Logistic probes on mean-pooled codes; importance = |w_j|·E[c_j]","Size-matched group ablation (zeroing codes), with frozen-probe and retrained variants"],"results":["Selectivity–importance mean Pearson r = 0.107 [0.068, 0.146] over 21 settings","|r| ≤ 0.32 in all nine BCI-middle seed retrainings","Frozen-probe ΔBA: specialists +0.0055 [−0.007, 0.027]; fragile −0.028 [−0.051, −0.003]; random −0.019 [−0.033, −0.008]","Effects shrink after probe retraining","Probe balanced accuracy spans 0.236–0.625"],"conditions":["Ablation ordering is seed-dependent on BCI middle","Fragile latents fire 8.9× more than specialists, so readout groups are unmatched on baseline activity","Linear probe only; 21/27 settings (REVE MA and Speech exports missing)"]},{"id":"c4","text":"Independent observational validation on clean EEG fails in the intended direction. Specialist latents do not fire more on high-alpha trials; on average they are slightly anti-correlated with relative alpha power.","methods":["Correlate each latent's clean activation with trial-wise relative alpha power, a quantity not used in selection","Activity-matched non-specialist controls, nearest in clean firing rate and mean activation, drawn without replacement","Top-five exemplar analysis with Welch spectra (secondary)"],"results":["Specialist mean |r| 0.143 vs fragile 0.246 (fragile higher in 26/27 settings) vs random 0.097","Specialist signed r = −0.073, negative in 23/27 settings","Activity-matched controls: |r| 0.143 vs 0.101, specialist edge in 27/27 settings; Δ|r| CI [0.032, 0.052]; matched firing 0.374 vs 0.374","Top-activating exemplars: specialists +0.012 relative alpha over fragile exemplars, higher in only 12/27 settings"],"conditions":["Relative band power tests only a global frequency-detector reading","Structured spatial–spectral features are not ruled out"]},{"id":"c5","text":"A forked validation ladder sets out which evidence supports which claim. Stages 1–3 (sensitivity, distortion control, specificity) plus independent observational validation support a representational claim. Readout intervention (stage 4) is needed only for the stronger task-relevance claim.","methods":["Table 1 maps each kind of evidence to the claim it supports","Figure 1 shows the fork in the ladder"],"results":["In this case study neither the representational claim nor the task-relevance claim is supported","Responding to alpha removal supports only 'alpha-sensitive'"],"conditions":["The ladder is an operational protocol for excluding alternatives, not a universal feature finder","No positive control has been run yet","Nothing in the ladder establishes neural causality"]},{"id":"c6","text":"Channel-dropout robustness of SAE codes decreases with depth in all nine backbone–dataset combinations, most strongly for DINOv3.","methods":["Random and contiguous channel-dropout perturbations","Late-minus-early active-set Jaccard"],"results":["Mean late-minus-early Jaccard: −0.17 (random dropout), −0.20 (contiguous dropout)","Contiguous ΔJaccard: DINOv3 ≈ −0.35, CBraMod ≈ −0.19, REVE ≈ −0.07"],"conditions":["Reported as a secondary architectural observation in Appendix C"]},{"id":"c7","text":"The validation problem is not specific to EEG-pretrained models; it persists when EEG is encoded by a vision-pretrained foundation model.","methods":["DINOv3 ViT-B/16 receives channel-by-time EEG images (prefix tokens excluded)","DINOv3 dictionary width reduced to 4× or 8× where token support is limited"],"results":["DINOv3 raw alpha/sham ratio 5.1, alongside CBraMod 7.4 and REVE 8.9","Spectral-normalized ratio >1 in 0/27 settings, which include all DINOv3 settings"],"conditions":["One SAE seed for every setting except BCI middle"]}],
"items":[
{"id":"q1","type":"failure","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"The collapse of the alpha/sham ratio under spectral-energy normalization depends on a property of the EEG spectrum. Would the normalization still turn a large raw ratio into a ratio below one if the EEG spectrum were flat across 8–12 Hz and 30–34 Hz, and why?","answer":"No. With a flat spectrum, the alpha and sham notches would remove roughly equal energy, so the removed-energy ratio would be near 1. Dividing by it would leave the raw advantage largely intact. The collapse happens only because the 1/f spectrum makes the alpha notch remove 11.8–57.2× more energy than the sham.","rubric":["States that the collapse would not occur, or that the raw advantage would largely remain","Explains that the removed-energy ratio would be near 1 because, under a flat spectrum, both notches remove similar energy","Ties the actual collapse to the 1/f spectrum making the alpha notch remove much more energy"]},
{"id":"q2","type":"failure","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"The fragile groups produce a larger frozen-probe accuracy drop than the specialist groups. Under what condition would this gap stop being evidence that fragile latents are intrinsically more important to the readout, and why?","answer":"The gap stops being such evidence when the groups differ in baseline activity, as they do here: fragile latents fire 8.9× more. Importance is |w_j|·E[c_j], and zeroing a high-activity latent removes more input to the probe. The larger drop may therefore reflect activity rather than intrinsic relevance, and the comparison would only be clean if the groups were matched on activity.","rubric":["Identifies unmatched baseline activity (fragile latents fire 8.9× more) as the condition","Explains that zeroing high-activity latents removes more probe input, so importance is confounded with activity (for example via the E[c_j] term)"]},
{"id":"q3","type":"failure","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Would the paper's independent observational validation reliably detect a latent that encodes alpha only over a small cluster of channels, and why?","answer":"Not reliably. The validation correlates activation with trial-wise relative alpha power, a global spectral quantity. Alpha confined to a few channels could vary independently of global relative alpha, so a localized alpha latent might show a weak correlation and be missed. The paper says these tests do not rule out structured spatial–spectral features.","rubric":["Says the test would not reliably detect such a latent, or might miss it","Explains that relative alpha power is a global quantity that can miss channel-localized alpha structure"]},
{"id":"q4","type":"failure","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"The conclusion that alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent leans most heavily on the spectral-energy normalization. If SAE responses actually scaled with time-domain distortion rather than with removed spectral energy, would that conclusion still hold as strongly, and why?","answer":"It would hold less strongly. Under time-domain normalization the ratio is 1.32 (CI [1.12, 1.55]) and exceeds one in 17/27 settings, which leaves a modest residual alpha advantage rather than a reversal. This is why the paper says the two normalizations bracket the confound rather than settle it.","rubric":["Says the conclusion would be weaker, or that a modest alpha advantage would remain","Cites the time-normalized ratio of about 1.32 and/or >1 in 17/27 settings, with a CI above 1"]},
{"id":"q5","type":"failure","claims":["c3","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"The selectivity score subtracts the mean response over the other five bands. Would it reliably exclude a latent that responds equally strongly to alpha and to theta and to nothing else, and why?","answer":"No. The theta response is averaged with four near-zero bands, so only one fifth of it is subtracted from the alpha response. The latent keeps a high alpha selectivity and could land in the top quartile despite not being alpha-specific.","rubric":["Says the latent would not be reliably excluded, or could still be labeled alpha-selective","Explains that a single competing band contributes only one fifth of its response to the subtracted mean"]},
{"id":"q6","type":"failure","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Would it be safe to treat the paper's specialist-versus-fragile-versus-random ablation ordering as a stable ranking for a single new setting with one SAE seed, and why?","answer":"No. The ordering is seed-dependent even on the BCI-middle setting, and the specialist effect's CI spans zero ([−0.007, 0.027]). Effects also shrink after probe retraining. A single-seed setting could therefore show a different ordering.","rubric":["Says it is not safe","Cites seed dependence of the ordering and/or the specialist CI including zero"]},
{"id":"q7","type":"why","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does dividing by time-domain distortion leave the alpha/sham ratio above one (1.32), while dividing by removed spectral energy drives it to 0.28?","answer":"Time-domain distortion is a norm of the removed signal, which grows more slowly than the removed energy itself. The alpha notch's much larger energy removal therefore enlarges the time-domain denominator less than it enlarges the spectral-energy denominator. The time-domain correction removes less of the raw 7.3× advantage.","rubric":["States that the time-domain denominator penalizes the alpha notch less than the spectral-energy denominator","Explains this by the time-domain measure being a norm (amplitude-like) that scales more slowly than removed energy"]},
{"id":"q8","type":"why","claims":["c4","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the activity-matched comparison, rather than the comparison with fragile latents, give the fair test of whether specialists track clean alpha more than other latents?","answer":"Fragile latents fire much more (8.9×) and have higher |r| (0.246), so their advantage is confounded with baseline activity. Matched controls equalize clean firing (0.374 vs 0.374) and mean activation, which isolates whether the selection procedure itself picks alpha-tracking latents.","rubric":["Says fragile latents differ in baseline activity, which confounds |r|","Explains that matched controls equalize firing and activation, isolating the effect of selection"]},
{"id":"q9","type":"why","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Specialists show a small |r| edge over activity-matched controls in 27/27 settings. Why does this edge still fail to support an alpha-detector reading?","answer":"|r| is unsigned. The signed correlation is negative on average (−0.073, negative in 23/27 settings), so specialists tend to fire on trials with less relative alpha, the opposite of what an alpha detector would do.","rubric":["Notes that |r| ignores direction","Cites the negative signed correlation (about −0.073, 23/27 settings), meaning specialists fire more when alpha is lower"]},
{"id":"q10","type":"why","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the positive mean frozen-probe change of +0.0055 after zeroing specialists not show that specialists harm the classifier?","answer":"Its 95% CI [−0.007, 0.027] includes zero, so the effect is indistinguishable from no change. The ordering is also seed-dependent, and the effects shrink after retraining.","rubric":["States that the effect is not distinguishable from zero","Cites the CI spanning zero"]},
{"id":"q11","type":"why","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"REVE has the largest raw alpha/sham ratio of any backbone. Why is it unsurprising that spectral normalization still pushes alpha below one even for REVE?","answer":"REVE's mean raw ratio of 8.9 is smaller than even the smallest dataset removed-energy ratio (11.8 on Speech), and much smaller than 34.6 and 57.2. Dividing a ratio near 9 by any of these gives a value below 1, consistent with 0/27 settings exceeding one.","rubric":["Compares REVE's raw ratio (8.9) with the removed-energy ratios, noting that even the smallest (11.8) is larger","Concludes that the normalized ratio is therefore below 1"]},
{"id":"q12","type":"why","claims":["c1","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why might a latent show a nonzero |Δf| under the alpha band-stop even if its own pre-activation barely changed?","answer":"The SAE keeps only the top k=32 pre-activations. If the perturbation raises other latents' pre-activations enough, they can push this latent out of the active set, changing its firing through rank displacement rather than through its own response.","rubric":["Attributes the change to TopK competition or rank displacement","Explains that other latents rising can push it out of, or into, the top-32 active set"]},
{"id":"q13","type":"why","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Why do the paper's confidence intervals resample settings rather than individual latents?","answer":"The claims are about whether an effect replicates across backbone–dataset–depth settings. Latents within a setting share one dictionary and backbone, so they are not independent replicates. Treating thousands of latents as independent would give misleadingly narrow intervals.","rubric":["States that the setting is the unit of replication, or that latents within a setting are not independent","Notes that latent-level resampling would understate uncertainty, or overstate precision"]},
{"id":"q14","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":"p1","question":"If the sham notch were moved from 30–34 Hz to 13–17 Hz, would you expect the raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio to be smaller than 7.3?","answer":"Yes. Under the 1/f spectrum a 13–17 Hz notch removes more energy than a 30–34 Hz notch, so the sham response would grow and the raw ratio would shrink. This follows the paper's finding that the response tracks removed energy.","rubric":["Answers yes, a smaller ratio","Reasons that a lower-frequency sham removes more energy under 1/f, enlarging the sham response"]},
{"id":"q15","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":"p1","question":"If the sham notch were moved from 30–34 Hz to 60–64 Hz, would you expect the raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio to be smaller than 7.3?","answer":"No, it would likely be larger. A higher-frequency sham removes even less energy under the 1/f spectrum, so the sham response shrinks and the raw ratio inflates, even though the alpha response is unchanged.","rubric":["Answers no, the ratio would likely be larger","Reasons that a higher-frequency sham removes less energy under 1/f"]},
{"id":"q16","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p2","question":"A latent passes stages 1–3 and independent observational validation, but zeroing it does not change an imagined-speech probe. Does the ladder still support calling it an alpha-representing latent?","answer":"Yes. Under the forked ladder, stage 4 (readout intervention) is required only for the stronger task-relevance claim. Stages 1–3 plus observational validation suffice for the representational claim.","rubric":["Answers yes","Explains that readout intervention is a side branch needed only for task relevance, not for representation"]},
{"id":"q17","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p2","question":"A latent passes stages 1–3 and a readout intervention changes task behavior, but it fails independent observational validation. Does the ladder support calling it an alpha-representing latent?","answer":"No. The representational path requires that the property be visible in clean, unperturbed data. Readout relevance does not substitute for that, and Table 1's task-relevant row also builds on observational validation.","rubric":["Answers no","Explains that observational validation on clean data is required for the representational claim and that readout evidence cannot replace it"]},
{"id":"q18","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c4","c5"],"pair":"p3","question":"Suppose specialists kept their |r| edge over activity-matched controls, but their signed correlation with relative alpha power were positive in most settings. Would they pass the independent observational validation stage?","answer":"Yes, for that stage. Specialists would then covary with clean alpha in the intended direction beyond activity-matched controls, which is what this stage asks. The full representational claim would still need the earlier stages, including distortion control.","rubric":["Answers yes for the observational stage","Reasons that positive covariation beyond matched controls is the intended direction"]},
{"id":"q19","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c4","c5"],"pair":"p3","question":"Suppose specialists kept their |r| edge over activity-matched controls, but their signed correlation with relative alpha power were negative in most settings. Would they pass the independent observational validation stage?","answer":"No. A negative signed correlation means they fire more when alpha is lower, which contradicts an alpha-detector reading despite the |r| edge. This is the paper's actual result (−0.073, 23/27 settings).","rubric":["Answers no","Reasons that negative signed r is the wrong direction for an alpha detector, so the unsigned edge does not count"]},
{"id":"q20","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p4","question":"On the Speech dataset (removed-energy ratio 11.8), would a raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio of 9 exceed one after spectral-energy normalization?","answer":"No. 9 / 11.8 ≈ 0.76, which is below one.","rubric":["Answers no","Shows the division 9 / 11.8 ≈ 0.76 < 1"]},
{"id":"q21","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p4","question":"On the Speech dataset (removed-energy ratio 11.8), would a raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio of 15 exceed one after spectral-energy normalization?","answer":"Yes. 15 / 11.8 ≈ 1.27, which is above one.","rubric":["Answers yes","Shows the division 15 / 11.8 ≈ 1.27 > 1"]},
{"id":"q22","type":"transfer","claims":["c1","c2","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"In an ECG foundation model, a team finds an SAE latent whose firing changes 10× more when a low-frequency band is removed than when an equal-width high-frequency sham band is removed. Following the paper, what is the first check needed before calling it a band-specific feature, and why?","answer":"The team should first normalize the response by how much signal each removal deletes, using spectral energy and/or time-domain distortion. If the low-frequency band carries much more power, the 10× gap may simply reflect larger distortion, as with alpha's 7.3× that became 0.28×.","rubric":["Names distortion or energy normalization (the stage-2 control) as the needed check","Explains that unequal power across bands can inflate the raw ratio, analogous to the alpha case"]},
{"id":"q23","type":"transfer","claims":["c5","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team wants to claim that latent j is a 'task-relevant alpha representation' for a motor-imagery classifier. Is a group ablation showing an accuracy drop sufficient, and why?","answer":"No. In Table 1 the task-relevant row requires everything above it: response, survival of distortion and competing-perturbation controls, and clean-data covariation with alpha. An ablation alone shows only readout relevance, not that the latent represents alpha.","rubric":["Answers no","Explains that the task-relevant claim also requires stages 1–3 and observational validation in addition to the readout intervention"]},
{"id":"q24","type":"transfer","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"A team will deploy SAE codes from EEG headsets that often lose contiguous channels. Based on the paper, which depth should they extract codes from, and which backbone shows the smallest depth-related loss of stability?","answer":"They should prefer early layers, since late-layer Jaccard under dropout is lower in all nine combinations. REVE shows the mildest depth effect (contiguous ΔJaccard ≈ −0.07, against −0.35 for DINOv3).","rubric":["Recommends early layers","Names REVE as the least depth-sensitive backbone (≈ −0.07 vs DINOv3 ≈ −0.35)"]},
{"id":"q25","type":"transfer","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"On a new dataset the alpha notch removes only 3× more spectral energy than the sham, and the raw alpha/sham ratio is 7. Would this setting pass the paper's distortion control, and would that alone justify an 'alpha-representing' label?","answer":"It would pass the spectral distortion check, since 7 / 3 ≈ 2.3 > 1. That alone would not justify the label: the latent would still need to pass the specificity stage and independent observational validation on clean EEG.","rubric":["States that the normalized ratio exceeds one (≈ 2.3), so the distortion control is passed","States that further stages (specificity and clean-data validation) are still required for the representational label"]},
{"id":"q26","type":"transfer","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"A researcher examines only each specialist's top-activating trials and finds slightly higher alpha than in fragile latents' exemplars. Given the paper's results, should they conclude the specialists are alpha detectors?","answer":"No. The exemplar test conditions on activation extremes, which is why the paper treats the all-trial correlation as primary. In the paper the exemplar edge was tiny (+0.012, only 12/27 settings), while the all-trial signed r was negative.","rubric":["Answers no","Notes that top-exemplar analysis conditions on extremes, so all-trial correlation is primary, or cites the weak exemplar edge versus the negative all-trial r"]},
{"id":"q27","type":"transfer","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team wants to know whether an already-deployed, fixed linear classifier depends on a set of SAE latents. Which of the paper's ablation variants should they use, and why?","answer":"They should use the frozen-probe variant. It keeps the trained classifier fixed and ablates only at test time, so it measures the deployed head's reliance. The retrained variant refits the probe, which can recover the information from other latents; this is why effects shrink after retraining.","rubric":["Chooses the frozen-probe variant","Explains that retraining lets the probe compensate, so it does not measure the fixed head's dependence"]},
{"id":"q28","type":"transfer","claims":["c1","c2","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"A team plans to label beta-band features by comparing a 13–30 Hz band-stop against a width-matched notch in the high-gamma range. Based on the paper, what bias should they expect in the raw ratio?","answer":"They should expect an inflated raw ratio favoring beta. Under the 1/f spectrum the lower-frequency notch removes more energy than a high-frequency sham, so part of the raw advantage would reflect distortion and would need normalization.","rubric":["Predicts the raw ratio is biased upward in favor of the lower band","Attributes this to the 1/f spectrum causing larger energy removal by the lower-frequency notch"]},
{"id":"q29","type":"connect","claims":["c2","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"If the spectral-energy-normalized alpha/sham ratio had exceeded one in most settings, which of the paper's stated contributions would lose its support, and which negative finding would still stand?","answer":"Contribution (ii), that the 7.3× signature is largely an artifact of input distortion, would lose support, because stage 2 would be passed. The observational failure (negative signed r with clean alpha) would still block the representational claim.","rubric":["Identifies the distortion-artifact claim (contribution ii, stage 2) as undermined","Notes that the clean-alpha observational failure would still stand"]},
{"id":"q30","type":"connect","claims":["c4","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"If specialists' signed correlation with relative alpha power had been clearly positive and above activity-matched controls, which conclusion stated in the abstract would lose its support?","answer":"The statement that latents selected for their response to alpha removal give no support for a simple alpha-detector reading. This is also the part of contribution (iii) saying the remaining latents do not track clean-EEG alpha in the intended direction.","rubric":["Names the 'no support for an alpha-detector reading' / 'do not track clean alpha in the intended direction' conclusion","Links it to the observational validation result (negative signed r)"]},
{"id":"q31","type":"connect","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If fragile and specialist groups had fired at similar baseline rates in the ablation, which caveat on the readout result would disappear?","answer":"The baseline-activity confound would disappear. The paper currently reads the ablation ordering only as a direction because fragile latents fire 8.9× more. With matched activity, the larger fragile drop could be read more directly as a difference in importance.","rubric":["Identifies the baseline-activity confound (the 8.9× firing difference) as the caveat removed","States that the ablation gap could then be interpreted more directly as differential importance"]},
{"id":"q32","type":"connect","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If some of the nine BCI-middle seed retrainings had shown a selectivity–importance correlation near 0.8, which claim would be weakened?","answer":"The claim that alpha selectivity is not readout importance would be weakened, specifically its robustness across SAE seeds. Its support includes the finding that coupling stays weak (|r| ≤ 0.32) in all nine retrainings.","rubric":["Names the claim that selectivity is not readout importance, or its seed robustness","Cites the |r| ≤ 0.32 in all nine retrainings as the evidence that would be contradicted"]},
{"id":"q33","type":"connect","claims":["c7","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"If DINOv3 had shown no raw alpha-over-sham advantage, which question that the paper uses DINOv3 to address would get a different answer?","answer":"The question of whether the validation problem is peculiar to EEG-pretrained representations. The misleading raw alpha signature would then appear only in EEG-native backbones rather than persisting in a vision-pretrained model.","rubric":["Identifies the question of whether the problem is EEG-pretraining-specific or persists cross-modally","States that the answer would shift toward 'EEG-specific'"]},
{"id":"q34","type":"connect","claims":["c6","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"If DINOv3's late layers had been more stable to channel dropout than its early layers, which Appendix C conclusion would be undermined?","answer":"The conclusion that useful transfer by a vision foundation model need not bring matching internal robustness, along with the claim that deeper SAE representations are less stable in both EEG-native and cross-modal backbones. That conclusion rests on DINOv3 showing the strongest depth-related drop (≈ −0.35).","rubric":["Names the 'vision FM transfer need not bring matching robustness' conclusion and/or the claim that depth instability holds across backbones","Cites DINOv3's strongest drop as its support"]},
{"id":"q35","type":"scope","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that its validation ladder can successfully accept a physiological label for some SAE latent? Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. In this case study neither claim is supported for any latent, and the positive control on another physiological axis that would test acceptance is left for future work.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Notes that no latent passed and no positive control was run"]},
{"id":"q36","type":"scope","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that alpha-specialist latents are unimportant to fine-tuned or nonlinear EEG classifiers? Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. Relevance was tested only with logistic probes on mean-pooled codes from frozen backbones; the paper says this does not speak to nonlinear or fine-tuned behavior.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Cites the restriction to linear probes on mean-pooled codes of frozen models"]},
{"id":"q37","type":"scope","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that these foundation models do not encode alpha activity in any SAE latent? Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. Only perturbation-selected specialists were tested, and only against global relative alpha power. Structured spatial–spectral alpha features, and latents chosen by other criteria, were not ruled out.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Notes the test covered only selected latents and/or only a global frequency reading"]},
{"id":"q38","type":"scope","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper support the claim that deeper layers of every tested backbone produce SAE codes less stable to channel dropout? Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.","answer":"Supported for the tested combinations. Late-layer Jaccard was lower than early-layer Jaccard in all nine backbone–dataset combinations, though the effect was only mild for REVE (≈ −0.07).","rubric":["Answers supported (within the tested backbones and datasets)","Cites all nine combinations showing lower late-layer overlap, possibly noting REVE's mild effect"]},

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu: Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford

###### Abstract

SAE latents in EEG foundation models are easy to name and easy to misname. Across 27 settings (3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths), alpha removal changes latent firing $7.3\times$ more than an equal-width sham notch. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio falls to $0.28\times$ and exceeds one in 0/27 settings. Alpha-responsive latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power. We propose a validation ladder with four checks: response, distortion control, specificity, and clean-data observation, plus a separate readout-relevance test. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what an SAE latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability. A latent whose firing changes after an alpha band-stop can be called an "alpha feature" without any check that it represents alpha.

Selection and evaluation use distinct quantities. Perturbation responses choose latents, and clean signals determine what they track.

The ladder (Figure 1; Table 1) has these stages:
- Stages 1–3 ask whether a response is sensitive, larger than the intervention's distortion, and specific rather than broadly fragile.
- Independent observational validation (stage 5) asks whether the property is visible without perturbation.
- Stages 1–3 plus 5 support only a representational claim.
- Readout intervention (stage 4) is a side branch. It is needed only for the stronger claim that the feature matters to a specified readout. A perfect alpha tracker could be useless for imagined speech and still be an alpha feature.

The individual diagnostics are ordinary scientific tests. What is new is identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation, plus an operational hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. The question is when a perturbation-responsive latent deserves a physiological label.

Contributions:
1. A forked validation protocol supporting claims of different strengths.
2. A 27-setting demonstration that a $7.3\times$ alpha signature is largely an input-distortion artifact.
3. Evidence that the remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean-EEG alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

Table 1: Evidence per stage and the claim it supports. None establish a causal neural mechanism.

| Evidence | Claim supported |
|---|---|
| Responds to alpha removal | Alpha-sensitive latent |
| Response survives distortion control and competing perturbations | Alpha-selective latent |
| Above, and independently covaries with alpha structure in clean EEG | Evidence for an alpha-representing latent |
| Above, and readout intervention changes task behavior | Task-relevant alpha representation |

Figure 1: Forked validation ladder (stages 1–3 + 5 = representational; stage 4 = task-head claim). In this case study neither claim is supported.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.
- Backbones (frozen): CBraMod, REVE (EEG-pretrained), and DINOv3 ViT-B/16. DINOv3 receives channel-by-time EEG images with prefix tokens excluded; it tests whether the problem persists across pretraining modality.
- Data: 200 Hz, fixed splits.
  - BCI IV 2a (BCI; motor imagery, 22 ch).
  - PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (MA; workload, 20 ch).
  - BCI Comp. 2020 Track 3 (Speech; imagined speech, 64 ch).
- A setting is backbone × dataset × depth, giving 27 settings.

#### TopK SAEs.

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

- $k=32$; loss is MSE + AuxK.
- Early/middle/late tokens are layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$.
- Expansion is $16\times$, except $4\times$/$8\times$ for DINOv3.
- Test FVU lies in $[0.059,0.228]$ with $L_0=32$.
- BCI middle is retrained under 3 seeds per backbone.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.
- Spatial: zero random channels or contiguous windows.
- Spectral: 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at $\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, high-$\gamma$, plus 8–12 Hz alpha vs. width-matched 30–34 Hz sham.
- Metrics: code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$.
- Under $1/f$ power, alpha/sham removed-energy ratios are 57.2/34.6/11.8 (BCI/MA/Speech). Responses are therefore divided by $\|x-\tilde{x}\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or by the removed spectral-energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.
- Selectivity: $s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$.
- Specialist-like: top-quartile alpha selectivity and ≤ median channel-dropout fragility.
- Controls: size-matched general-fragile and random groups (readout); activity-matched non-specialists, nearest in clean firing rate and mean activation without replacement (clean alpha).
- Probes: logistic, on mean-pooled codes.
- Importance: $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$.
- Group ablation: zero size-matched groups and measure Δ balanced accuracy, either test-time only (frozen probe) or with probe refit (retrained).
- Observational validation: clean activation vs. trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection), for 12,041 latents per group.
- CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task analyses).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

- Alpha changes firing 5–9× more than sham in every backbone and lowers overlap in 27/27 settings (App. B).
- Alpha is the max-$|\Delta f|$/min-Jaccard band in 15/27 settings: a plurality.

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings.

| $|\Delta f|$ ratio | Mean | 95% CI | Settings $>1$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 7.33 | $[6.18,8.68]$ | 27/27 |
| per unit time-domain distortion | 1.32 | $[1.12,1.55]$ | 17/27 |
| per unit removed spectral energy | 0.28 | $[0.22,0.36]$ | 0/27 |

The two normalizations bracket the effect; the energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets. Alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent. Code-overlap ratios: raw 2.77, normalized 0.51 and 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

- Probe BA spans 0.236–0.625, so comparisons are within-setting.
- Selectivity–importance: $r=0.107$ (CI $[0.068,0.146]$, 21 settings; Fig. 2A); $|r|\le0.32$ in all nine BCI-middle retrainings.
- Frozen-probe ΔBA from zeroing:
  - specialist-like: $+0.0055$ ($[-0.007,0.027]$)
  - fragile: $-0.028$ ($[-0.051,-0.003]$)
  - random: $-0.019$ ($[-0.033,-0.008]$)
- Effects shrink after retraining.
- The ordering is seed-dependent on BCI middle, and fragile latents fire $8.9\times$ more. Read only as a direction: specialists are not preferentially important to this linear readout. This says nothing about nonlinear or fine-tuned heads and is not required for a representational claim.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

- Top-activating trials: specialists exceed matched fragile exemplars by only $+0.012$ relative alpha (higher in 12/27).
- All trials, mean $|r|$ with relative alpha:
  - specialists 0.143
  - fragile 0.246 (26/27)
  - random 0.097 (Fig. 2B)
- Specialist signed $r$ is $-0.073$, negative in 23/27: they fire on lower-alpha trials.
- Activity matching (firing 0.374 vs. 0.374) leaves specialists a small $|r|$ edge (0.143 vs. 0.101; 27/27; $\Delta|r|$ CI $[0.032,0.052]$) but does not reverse the sign.
- "Specialist-like" names a perturbation response. Structured spatial–spectral features are not ruled out, only a simple global frequency-detector reading.

Figure 2: A, per-setting selectivity–importance $r$ (REVE task codes BCI only), means near 0. B, specialist vs. random mean $|r|$ with relative alpha.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; it is not a feature finder or a claim that no latent is interpretable. A positive control on another axis is left to future work.

Limits:
- one SAE seed elsewhere;
- readout groups activity-unmatched;
- $|\Delta f|$ may include TopK rank displacement;
- relative band power tests only a global reading;
- logistic probe on mean-pooled codes;
- task analyses 21/27 (REVE MA/Speech exports unavailable);
- band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator, and the normalizations only bound that confound.

No clinical or neural-causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

The $7.3\times$ alpha response fails distortion control, clean-alpha tracking, and readout relevance. SAE feature names should be justified by Table 1's evidence stage, not a perturbation response alone.

#### Ethics statement.
Public EEG reanalysis, no participants or clinical predictions; consent and ethics procedures are inherited from the original releases.

- Layer groups: blocks 0–3/4–7/8–11 (CBraMod, DINOv3), 0–6/7–14/15–21 (REVE), with per-layer $\ell_2$ normalization.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1. Claims. Do the abstract and introduction reflect contributions and scope? [Yes] They state empirical scope; Sections 3–4 separate observations from physiological or causal claims.

2. Limitations. Are limitations discussed? [Yes] Section 4 covers SAE seeds, TopK competition, activity matching, linear-probe scope, missing task-analysis settings, and dataset scope.

3. Theory assumptions and proofs. [N/A] Empirical only.

4. Experimental result reproducibility. [Yes] Section 2 gives models, splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, and probes; supplementary code has exact configurations.

5. Open access to data and code. [Yes] Datasets and backbones are public and cited; anonymized code is supplementary; checkpoints and raw EEG are omitted for size.

6. Experimental setting/details. [Yes] Section 2 reports split policy, preprocessing, SAE sparsity and expansion, perturbation bands, metrics, and classifier protocol; full training details are in the supplement.

7. Experiment statistical significance. [Yes] Percentile 95% CIs come from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27 or 21), not latents, covering alpha/sham ratios, selectivity–importance correlations, clean-alpha $|r|$ contrasts, and ablations. Initialization variability uses three seeds on BCI middle.

8. Experiments compute resources. [Yes] Appendix F: A100s, ~300 GPU-hours, excluding unused exploratory runs.

9. Code of ethics. [Yes] Public datasets, negative findings and limitations reported, no clinical or individual-level claims.

10. Broader impacts. [Yes] Section 4 motivates stricter validation of biosignal interpretations and limits findings to representation auditing, not clinical or neural causality.

11. Safeguards. [N/A] No new generative model, personal data, or high-risk dataset is released; only frozen models and aggregate results are analyzed.

12. Licenses for existing assets. [Yes] Section 2 cites releases; Appendix F lists licenses and terms for three datasets and three backbones.

13. New assets. [Yes] Supplementary code records configurations, output schemas, seeds, and run manifests.

14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects. [N/A] No participants or crowdsourcing.

15. IRB approvals or equivalent. [N/A] No new human-subject data; original public releases are cited.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models. Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu (Dept. of Engineering Science, University of Oxford)

**Abstract.** Across 27 settings (3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths), alpha removal changes SAE latent firing 7.3× more than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI [6.2,8.7], bootstrapped over settings), but the alpha filter deletes far more signal. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is 0.28× (CI [0.22,0.36]), >1 in 0/27 settings. Alpha-selected latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power (mean r=−0.073). We propose a validation ladder: does a latent respond; does it survive controlling for removed signal; is it specific rather than broadly fragile; is the property visible on unperturbed data; and, separately, does it matter to a task classifier. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what an SAE latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability: a latent moving after an alpha band-stop can be called an "alpha feature" unchecked. Selection and evaluation use distinct quantities: perturbation responses choose latents; clean signals determine what they track.

Ladder (Fig. 1, Table 1): Stages 1–3 test sensitivity, response beyond intervention distortion, and specificity vs. broad fragility; Stage 5 (independent observational validation) tests visibility without perturbation. Passing these supports only a representational claim. Stage 4 (readout intervention) is a side branch, needed only for functional relevance to a specified readout; a perfect alpha tracker useless for imagined speech is still an alpha feature. The diagnostics are ordinary; new is identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation and a hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. DINOv3 tests whether the problem persists for an FM pretrained in another modality.

Contributions: (i) a forked protocol supporting claims at different strengths; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that the 7.3× alpha signature is largely an input-distortion artifact; (iii) evidence that remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

Table 1: None establishes a causal neural mechanism.

| Evidence | Claim supported |
|---|---|
| Responds to alpha removal | Alpha-sensitive latent |
| Survives distortion control and competing perturbations | Alpha-selective latent |
| Above + independently covaries with alpha in clean EEG | Evidence for an alpha-representing latent |
| Above + readout intervention changes task behavior | Task-relevant alpha representation |

Figure 1: Forked ladder. Here neither claim is supported.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.
Frozen CBraMod, REVE, DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (channel×time EEG images, prefix tokens excluded). 200 Hz, fixed splits: BCI IV 2a (BCI; motor imagery, 22 ch), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (MA; workload, 20 ch), BCI 2020 Track 3 (Speech; imagined speech, 64 ch). Setting = backbone×dataset×depth (27).

#### TopK SAEs.
$c=\operatorname{ReLU}(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc})),\ \hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}$; k=32; MSE+AuxK. Early/middle/late tokens normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_2=\sqrt d$. Expansion 16× (some DINOv3 4×/8×). Test FVU ∈[0.059,0.228], $L_0$=32. BCI middle retrained ×3 seeds.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.
Paired perturbed test trials: zeroed random channels or contiguous windows; 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at δ,θ,α,β,γ, high-γ; 8–12 Hz alpha vs. 30–34 Hz sham. Metrics: code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$. Alpha/sham removed-energy ratios 57.2/34.6/11.8 (BCI/MA/Speech). Normalize by $\|x-\tilde x\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or removed spectral energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.
$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac15\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$. Specialist-like: top-quartile alpha selectivity, ≤ median dropout fragility. Readout contrasts: size-matched general-fragile, random; clean-alpha contrast: activity-matched non-specialists. Logistic probes on mean-pooled codes; importance $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$. Group ablation zeros codes, Δ balanced accuracy (frozen clean-trained probe or retrained). Validation: clean activation vs. trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection), 12,041 latents/group. CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control
Alpha changes firing 5–9× more than sham per backbone, lowering overlap in 27/27 (App. B). Alpha is max-$|\Delta f|$/min-Jaccard band in 15/27 (plurality). Dropout robustness falls with depth (App. C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio.

| Ratio | Mean | 95% CI | >1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 7.33 | [6.18,8.68] | 27/27 |
| per time-domain distortion | 1.32 | [1.12,1.55] | 17/27 |
| per removed spectral energy | 0.28 | [0.22,0.36] | 0/27 |

The normalizations bracket rather than settle (energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets), but show alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent. Overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then 0.51, 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance
Probe BA 0.236–0.625; compared within settings. Selectivity–importance r=0.107 (CI [0.068,0.146], 21 settings; Fig. 2A); |r|≤0.32 in all 9 BCI-middle retrainings. Frozen ΔBA: specialist +0.0055 [−0.007,0.027], fragile −0.028 [−0.051,−0.003], random −0.019 [−0.033,−0.008]; smaller after retraining. Ordering is seed-dependent and groups unmatched on activity (fragile fire 8.9× more): a direction only; silent on nonlinear/fine-tuned behavior.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction
Top-activating trials: specialists +0.012 relative alpha over fragile (12/27). All trials: specialist mean |r| 0.143 vs. fragile 0.246 (26/27), random 0.097 (Fig. 2B); signed r −0.073 (negative 23/27). Activity-matched (firing 0.374 vs. 0.374): 0.143 vs. 0.101 (27/27; Δ|r| CI [0.032,0.052]), sign unchanged. Spatial–spectral features not ruled out, only a global frequency-detector reading.

Figure 2: A: per-setting selectivity–importance r (REVE: BCI only), means near 0. B: mean |r|, specialists vs. random.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; not a universal feature finder nor a claim that no latent is interpretable. Positive control left to future work. Limits: one SAE seed elsewhere; ablation groups activity-unmatched; $|\Delta f|$ may include TopK rank displacement; global band power only; logistic probe on mean-pooled codes; task analyses 21/27 (REVE MA/Speech missing); band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator. No clinical/causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

Semantic SAE labels should be justified by the Table 1 stage, not perturbation response alone.

#### Ethics statement.
Reanalysis of public EEG; no participants; no clinical predictions; consent inherited.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu — Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford

###### Abstract

SAE latents are easy to interpret and to misinterpret. Across 27 settings (3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths), alpha removal changes latent firing 7.3× more than an equal-width sham notch. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is 0.28× and exceeds one in no setting. Alpha-responsive latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power. We propose a validation ladder: response, distortion control, specificity, observational validation on unperturbed data, and, separately, task-readout relevance. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what a latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability. A latent that moves after an alpha band-stop gets called an "alpha feature" without anyone checking that it represents alpha. That signature appears in all 27 settings: frozen CBraMod, REVE and DINOv3, at early, middle and late depth, on three public EEG tasks. One input-distortion control overturns it, and the latents that survive fail an independent check. Selection uses perturbation responses; evaluation uses clean signals.

The ladder (Fig. 1; Table 1) has five stages:
- **Stages 1–3:** Is the response sensitive, larger than the intervention's distortion, and specific rather than broadly fragile?
- **Stage 5:** Independent observational validation: is the property visible without perturbation? Passing stages 1–3 and 5 supports only a representational claim.
- **Stage 4:** Readout intervention is a side branch. It is needed only for the stronger claim of functional relevance to a specified readout. An alpha tracker that is useless for imagined speech is still an alpha feature.

No single diagnostic is new. What is new is identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation, plus a hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. Our question is when a perturbation-responsive latent deserves a physiological label. DINOv3 tests whether the problem persists for a foundation model pretrained in another modality.

Contributions:
- (i) a forked protocol that supports claims of different strengths;
- (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that the 7.3× signature is largely a distortion artifact;
- (iii) evidence that the remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

|Responds to alpha removal|Alpha-sensitive latent|
|Response survives distortion control and competing perturbations|Alpha-selective latent|

$c=\operatorname{ReLU}(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc})),\ \hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}$

- $k=32$; loss is MSE plus AuxK.
- Early/middle/late tokens are layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_2=\sqrt d$.
- Expansion 16×; DINOv3 uses 4×/8× (token support).
- 27 dictionaries: test FVU $[0.059,0.228]$, $L_0=32$.
- BCI middle of each backbone is retrained with 3 seeds.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

- **Pairs:** clean test trial vs. perturbed copy; SAEs frozen.
- **Spatial:** zero random channels or contiguous windows.
- **Spectral:** 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at $\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, high-$\gamma$; 8–12 Hz alpha vs. width-matched 30–34 Hz sham.
- **Metrics:** code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$.
- **Normalization:** under $1/f$ power the alpha notch removes far more (removed-energy ratios 57.2/34.6/11.8, BCI/MA/Speech). We divide by $\|x-\tilde x\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or by the removed spectral-energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

- **Selectivity:** $s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac15\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$.
- **Specialist-like:** top-quartile alpha selectivity and ≤ median channel-dropout fragility.
- **Controls:** size-matched general-fragile and random (readout); activity-matched non-specialists, nearest in clean firing rate and mean activation, no replacement (clean alpha).
- **Probes:** logistic on mean-pooled codes; importance $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$.
- **Group ablation:** zero a size-matched group; measure Δ balanced accuracy (BA). Frozen probe (trained clean, ablated at test) or retrained after ablation.
- **Observational validation:** clean activation vs. trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection), 12,041 latents per group.
- **CIs:** percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task analyses).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

- Alpha removal changes firing 5–9× more than sham per backbone and lowers overlap in all 27 settings (App. B).
- In the six-band sweep, alpha is the max-$|\Delta f|$/min-Jaccard band in 15/27, a plurality.
- Dropout robustness falls with depth (App. C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings.

|Ratio|Mean|95% CI|>1|
|-|-|-|-|
|raw|7.33|[6.18,8.68]|27/27|
|per time-domain distortion|1.32|[1.12,1.55]|17/27|
|per removed spectral energy|0.28|[0.22,0.36]|0/27|

The two normalizations bracket rather than settle the question; the energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets. They do show the response is not distortion-independent. Overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then 0.51 and 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe BA spans 0.236–0.625, so comparisons are within setting.
- **Selectivity–importance:** $r=0.107$ [0.068,0.146] over 21 settings (Fig. 2A); $|r|\le0.32$ in all nine BCI-middle retrainings.
- **Frozen ΔBA:** specialists +0.0055 [−0.007,0.027]; fragile −0.028 [−0.051,−0.003]; random −0.019 [−0.033,−0.008]. Effects shrink after retraining.

The ordering is seed-dependent (BCI middle), and fragile latents fire 8.9× more, so this is a direction only. Specialists are not preferentially important to this linear readout. This says nothing about nonlinear or fine-tuned behavior and is not needed for a representational claim.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

- **Top-activating trials:** specialists +0.012 relative alpha over matched fragile exemplars (12/27).
- **All trials, mean $|r|$:** specialists 0.143, fragile 0.246 (26/27), random 0.097 (Fig. 2B).
- **Signed $r$:** specialists −0.073 (negative in 23/27).
- **Activity-matched** (firing 0.374 vs. 0.374): specialists 0.143 vs. 0.101 (27/27; App. E). The sign is unchanged.

"Specialist-like" names a perturbation response, not a detector. Structured spatial–spectral features are not ruled out; only a global frequency-detector reading is.

Figure 2: A: per-setting $r$, selectivity vs. importance; means near 0 (REVE task codes BCI only). B: per-setting mean $|r|$, specialists vs. random.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; it is not a universal feature finder. The 7.3× signature fails, not SAE interpretability generally. A positive control on another axis is deferred.

Limits:
- one SAE seed elsewhere;
- readout groups activity-unmatched;
- $|\Delta f|$ may include TopK rank displacement;
- band power tests only global frequency;
- relevance means a logistic probe on mean-pooled codes;
- readouts 21/27 (no REVE MA/Speech exports);
- band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator; normalizations only bound this.

No clinical or causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

The 7.3× alpha response fails distortion control and marks neither clean-alpha trackers nor readout-critical units. Name features by evidence stage (Table 1).

#### Ethics statement.

Public EEG reanalysis; no participants or clinical predictions.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models. Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu (Dept. of Engineering Science, University of Oxford)

**Abstract.** Across 27 settings (3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths), alpha removal changes SAE latent firing 7.3× more than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI [6.2,8.7], bootstrapped over settings), but the alpha filter deletes far more signal. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is 0.28× (CI [0.22,0.36]), >1 in 0/27 settings. Alpha-selected latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power (mean r=−0.073). We propose a validation ladder: does a latent respond; does it survive controlling for removed signal; is it specific rather than broadly fragile; is the property visible on unperturbed data; and, separately, does it matter to a task classifier. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what an SAE latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability: a latent moving after an alpha band-stop can be called an "alpha feature" unchecked. Selection and evaluation use distinct quantities: perturbation responses choose latents; clean signals determine what they track.

Ladder (Fig. 1, Table 1): Stages 1–3 test sensitivity, response beyond intervention distortion, and specificity vs. broad fragility; Stage 5 (independent observational validation) tests visibility without perturbation. Passing these supports only a representational claim. Stage 4 (readout intervention) is a side branch, needed only for functional relevance to a specified readout; a perfect alpha tracker useless for imagined speech is still an alpha feature. The diagnostics are ordinary; new is identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation and a hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. DINOv3 tests whether the problem persists for an FM pretrained in another modality.

Contributions: (i) a forked protocol supporting claims at different strengths; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that the 7.3× alpha signature is largely an input-distortion artifact; (iii) evidence that remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

Table 1: None establishes a causal neural mechanism.

| Evidence | Claim supported |
|---|---|
| Responds to alpha removal | Alpha-sensitive latent |
| Survives distortion control and competing perturbations | Alpha-selective latent |
| Above + independently covaries with alpha in clean EEG | Evidence for an alpha-representing latent |
| Above + readout intervention changes task behavior | Task-relevant alpha representation |

Figure 1: Forked ladder. Here neither claim is supported.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.
Frozen CBraMod, REVE, DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (channel×time EEG images, prefix tokens excluded). 200 Hz, fixed splits: BCI IV 2a (BCI; motor imagery, 22 ch), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (MA; workload, 20 ch), BCI 2020 Track 3 (Speech; imagined speech, 64 ch). Setting = backbone×dataset×depth (27).

#### TopK SAEs.
$c=\operatorname{ReLU}(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc})),\ \hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}$; k=32; MSE+AuxK. Early/middle/late tokens normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_2=\sqrt d$. Expansion 16× (some DINOv3 4×/8×). Test FVU ∈[0.059,0.228], $L_0$=32. BCI middle retrained ×3 seeds.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.
Paired perturbed test trials: zeroed random channels or contiguous windows; 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at δ,θ,α,β,γ, high-γ; 8–12 Hz alpha vs. 30–34 Hz sham. Metrics: code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$. Alpha/sham removed-energy ratios 57.2/34.6/11.8 (BCI/MA/Speech). Normalize by $\|x-\tilde x\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or removed spectral energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.
$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac15\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$. Specialist-like: top-quartile alpha selectivity, ≤ median dropout fragility. Readout contrasts: size-matched general-fragile, random; clean-alpha contrast: activity-matched non-specialists. Logistic probes on mean-pooled codes; importance $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$. Group ablation zeros codes, Δ balanced accuracy (frozen clean-trained probe or retrained). Validation: clean activation vs. trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection), 12,041 latents/group. CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control
Alpha changes firing 5–9× more than sham per backbone, lowering overlap in 27/27 (App. B). Alpha is max-$|\Delta f|$/min-Jaccard band in 15/27 (plurality). Dropout robustness falls with depth (App. C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio.

| Ratio | Mean | 95% CI | >1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 7.33 | [6.18,8.68] | 27/27 |
| per time-domain distortion | 1.32 | [1.12,1.55] | 17/27 |
| per removed spectral energy | 0.28 | [0.22,0.36] | 0/27 |

The normalizations bracket rather than settle (energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets), but show alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent. Overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then 0.51, 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance
Probe BA 0.236–0.625; compared within settings. Selectivity–importance r=0.107 (CI [0.068,0.146], 21 settings; Fig. 2A); |r|≤0.32 in all 9 BCI-middle retrainings. Frozen ΔBA: specialist +0.0055 [−0.007,0.027], fragile −0.028 [−0.051,−0.003], random −0.019 [−0.033,−0.008]; smaller after retraining. Ordering is seed-dependent and groups unmatched on activity (fragile fire 8.9× more): a direction only; silent on nonlinear/fine-tuned behavior.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction
Top-activating trials: specialists +0.012 relative alpha over fragile (12/27). All trials: specialist mean |r| 0.143 vs. fragile 0.246 (26/27), random 0.097 (Fig. 2B); signed r −0.073 (negative 23/27). Activity-matched (firing 0.374 vs. 0.374): 0.143 vs. 0.101 (27/27; Δ|r| 0.042, CI [0.032,0.052]), sign unchanged. Spatial–spectral features not ruled out, only a global frequency-detector reading.

Figure 2: A: per-setting selectivity–importance r (REVE: BCI only), means near 0. B: mean |r|, specialists vs. random.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; not a universal feature finder nor a claim that no latent is interpretable. Positive control left to future work. Limits: one SAE seed elsewhere; ablation groups activity-unmatched; $|\Delta f|$ may include TopK rank displacement; global band power only; logistic probe on mean-pooled codes; task analyses 21/27 (REVE MA/Speech missing); band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator. No clinical/causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

Semantic SAE labels should be justified by the Table 1 stage, not perturbation response alone.

Reanalysis of public EEG; no participants; no clinical predictions; consent inherited.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models. Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu (Dept. of Engineering Science, University of Oxford)

**Abstract.** Across 27 settings (3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths), alpha removal changes SAE latent firing 7.3× more than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI [6.2,8.7], bootstrapped over settings), but the alpha filter deletes far more signal. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is 0.28× (CI [0.22,0.36]), >1 in 0/27 settings. Alpha-selected latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power (mean r=−0.073). We propose a validation ladder: does a latent respond; does it survive controlling for removed signal; is it specific rather than broadly fragile; is the property visible on unperturbed data; and, separately, does it matter to a task classifier. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what an SAE latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability: a latent moving after an alpha band-stop can be called an "alpha feature" unchecked. Selection and evaluation use distinct quantities: perturbation responses choose latents; clean signals determine what they track.

Ladder (Fig. 1, Table 1): Stages 1–3 test sensitivity, response beyond intervention distortion, and specificity vs. broad fragility; Stage 5 (independent observational validation) tests visibility without perturbation. Passing these supports only a representational claim. Stage 4 (readout intervention) is a side branch, needed only for functional relevance to a specified readout; a perfect alpha tracker useless for imagined speech is still an alpha feature. The diagnostics are ordinary; new is identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation and a hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. DINOv3 tests whether the problem persists for an FM pretrained in another modality.

Contributions: (i) a forked protocol supporting claims at different strengths; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that the 7.3× alpha signature is largely an input-distortion artifact; (iii) evidence that remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

Table 1: None establishes a causal neural mechanism.

| Evidence | Claim supported |
|---|---|
| Responds to alpha removal | Alpha-sensitive latent |
| Survives distortion control and competing perturbations | Alpha-selective latent |
| Above + independently covaries with alpha in clean EEG | Evidence for an alpha-representing latent |
| Above + readout intervention changes task behavior | Task-relevant alpha representation |

Figure 1: Forked ladder. Here neither claim is supported.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.
Frozen CBraMod, REVE, DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (channel×time EEG images, prefix tokens excluded). 200 Hz, fixed splits: BCI IV 2a (BCI; motor imagery, 22 ch), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (MA; workload, 20 ch), BCI 2020 Track 3 (Speech; imagined speech, 64 ch). Setting = backbone×dataset×depth (27).

#### TopK SAEs.
$c=\operatorname{ReLU}(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc})),\ \hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}$; k=32; MSE+AuxK. Early/middle/late tokens normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_2=\sqrt d$. Expansion 16× (some DINOv3 4×/8×). Test FVU ∈[0.059,0.228], $L_0$=32. BCI middle retrained ×3 seeds.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.
Paired perturbed test trials: zeroed random channels or contiguous windows; 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at δ,θ,α,β,γ, high-γ; 8–12 Hz alpha vs. 30–34 Hz sham. Metrics: code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$. Alpha/sham removed-energy ratios 57.2/34.6/11.8 (BCI/MA/Speech). Normalize by $\|x-\tilde x\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or removed spectral energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.
$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac15\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$. Specialist-like: top-quartile alpha selectivity, ≤ median dropout fragility. Readout contrasts: size-matched general-fragile, random; clean-alpha contrast: activity-matched non-specialists. Logistic probes on mean-pooled codes; importance $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$. Group ablation zeros codes, Δ balanced accuracy (frozen clean-trained probe or retrained). Validation: clean activation vs. trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection), 12,041 latents/group. CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control
Alpha changes firing 5–9× more than sham per backbone, lowering overlap in 27/27 (App. B). Alpha is max-$|\Delta f|$/min-Jaccard band in 15/27 (plurality). Dropout robustness falls with depth (App. C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio.

| Ratio | Mean | 95% CI | >1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 7.33 | [6.18,8.68] | 27/27 |
| per time-domain distortion | 1.32 | [1.12,1.55] | 17/27 |
| per removed spectral energy | 0.28 | [0.22,0.36] | 0/27 |

The normalizations bracket rather than settle (energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets), but show alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent. Overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then 0.51, 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance
Probe BA 0.236–0.625; compared within settings. Selectivity–importance r=0.107 (CI [0.068,0.146], 21 settings; Fig. 2A); |r|≤0.32 in all 9 BCI-middle retrainings. Frozen ΔBA: specialist +0.0055 [−0.007,0.027], fragile −0.028 [−0.051,−0.003], random −0.019 [−0.033,−0.008]; smaller after retraining. Ordering is seed-dependent and groups unmatched on activity (fragile fire 8.9× more): a direction only; silent on nonlinear/fine-tuned behavior.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction
Top-activating trials: specialists +0.012 relative alpha over fragile (12/27). All trials: specialist mean |r| 0.143 vs. fragile 0.246 (26/27), random 0.097 (Fig. 2B); signed r −0.073 (negative 23/27). Activity-matched (firing 0.374 vs. 0.374): 0.143 vs. 0.101 (27/27; Δ|r| 0.042, CI [0.032,0.052]), sign unchanged. Spatial–spectral features not ruled out, only a global frequency-detector reading.

Figure 2: A: per-setting selectivity–importance r (REVE: BCI only), means near 0. B: mean |r|, specialists vs. random.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; not a universal feature finder nor a claim that no latent is interpretable. Positive control left to future work. Limits: one SAE seed elsewhere; ablation groups activity-unmatched; $|\Delta f|$ may include TopK rank displacement; global band power only; logistic probe on mean-pooled codes; task analyses 21/27 (REVE MA/Speech missing); band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator. No clinical/causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

Semantic SAE labels should be justified by the Table 1 stage, not perturbation response alone.

#### Ethics statement.
Reanalysis of public EEG; no participants; no clinical predictions; consent inherited.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1. **Claims.** Do abstract/introduction reflect contributions and scope? [Yes]. Abstract and introduction state empirical scope; Sections 3–4 distinguish observations from physiological or causal claims. Guidelines: claims, contributions, assumptions and limitations should be stated and match results and expected generalization; aspirational goals fine if marked unattained.

2. **Limitations.** [Yes]. Section 4 discusses SAE seeds, TopK competition, activity matching, linear-probe scope, missing task-analysis settings, dataset scope. Guidelines: state strong assumptions and robustness to violations, scope (datasets, runs), performance factors, computational efficiency and scaling, privacy/fairness; reviewers will not penalize honesty about limitations.

3. **Theory assumptions and proofs.** [N/A]. Empirical analyses only; no theoretical claims. Guidelines: theorems need numbered, cross-referenced statements, full assumptions, and proofs (sketch in main text if proof is in supplement).

4. **Experimental result reproducibility.** [Yes]. Section 2 gives models, splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, probe protocol; supplementary code holds exact configurations. Guidelines: reproducibility is required regardless of code release, via code, instructions, hosted model, or checkpoints; new algorithms/architectures must be fully described; closed models need some verification path.

5. **Open access to data and code.** [Yes]. Datasets and backbones are public and cited; an anonymized code archive with training and analysis scripts is supplied; checkpoints and raw EEG omitted for size. Guidelines: [No] is acceptable unless code is central; give exact commands, environment, data access and preparation, scripts for all results (note omissions); anonymize at submission.

6. **Experimental setting/details.** [Yes]. Section 2 reports split policy, preprocessing, SAE sparsity and expansion, perturbation bands, metrics, classifier protocol; full training details in supplement. Guidelines: core paper should give detail needed to understand results; full details may go in code/appendix.

7. **Experiment statistical significance.** [Yes]. Means for alpha/sham ratios, selectivity–importance correlations, clean-alpha |r| contrasts, and group ablations carry percentile 95% CIs from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task analyses); the unit is the setting, not the latent. Initialization variability is quantified for BCI middle under three SAE seeds. Guidelines: state variability captured, calculation method, assumptions, and whether SD or SEM; 1-sigma bars must be stated; prefer 2-sigma over claiming a 96% CI if normality is unverified; avoid symmetric bars yielding out-of-range values; explain bars in text.

8. **Experiments compute resources.** [Yes]. Appendix F: NVIDIA A100s on a shared academic Slurm cluster, ~300 GPU-hours, excluding unused exploratory runs. Guidelines: give worker type, memory/storage, per-run and total compute, and whether the full project used more.

9. **Code of ethics.** [Yes]. Reanalysis of public research datasets, reports negative findings and limitations, no clinical or individual-level claims. Guidelines: explain any deviation; preserve anonymity.

10. **Broader impacts.** [Yes]. Section 4 motivates stricter validation of biosignal interpretations and limits findings to representation auditing, not clinical or neural causality. Guidelines: discuss positive and negative impacts (misuse, fairness, privacy, security), harms from correct, incorrect, or misused operation, and mitigations where a direct path to harm exists.

12. **Licenses for existing assets.** [Yes]. Section 2 cites original dataset releases; Appendix F lists licenses/terms for the three datasets and three backbone checkpoints. Guidelines: cite originals, give version/URL and license name, terms for scraped sources, and original plus derived licenses for repackaged data.

13. **New assets.** [Yes]. SAE training and analysis code records configurations, output schemas, random seeds, run manifests in the supplementary repository. Guidelines: document training, license, limitations, consent; anonymize at submission.

14. **Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects.** [N/A]. Secondary analysis; no participants or crowdsourcing. Guidelines: include instructions, screenshots, compensation (at least minimum wage).

15. **IRB approvals or equivalent.** [N/A]. No new human-subject data; Section 2 and Appendix F cite original public releases. Guidelines: state IRB approval where required; follow institutional rules; keep anonymity.

16. **Declaration of LLM usage.** [N/A]. LLM assistance limited to writing and formatting, not part of the scientific method. Guidelines: declare only if LLMs are an important, original, or non-standard methodological component.

Upon normalization by Q2H, the ratio by which alpha removal changes latent firing falls to $0.28\times$ (95% CI $[0.22,0.36]$) and exceeds one in none of the 27 settings, whereas before any such normalization this same change, measured across 27 settings spanning three backbones, three EEG datasets, and three network depths, has alpha removal changing latent firing $7.3\times$ more than an equal-width M5X (95% CI $[6.2,8.7]$, bootstrapped over settings), a figure under which the interpretation initially appears compelling. For semantic interpretations of Q7M latents, ZX4 is proposed, which asks in turn whether a latent responds, whether that response survives controlling for how much signal the intervention removes, whether it is specific rather than broadly fragile, and whether the proposed property is visible on unperturbed data, while the stronger claim that the latent matters to a task classifier is tested separately. Latents selected for their response to alpha removal are, on clean EEG, slightly anti-correlated with E7V (mean $r=-0.073$), giving no support for a simple alpha-detector reading, and the alpha filter also deletes far more signal than the M5X (M5X denoting the paper's sham notch); perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what a Q7M latent represents. The decomposition of dense model activations into discrete latents effected by Q7M makes individual features easy to interpret and easy to misinterpret, giving rise, in EEG foundation models, to the tempting inference that if removing alpha-band activity strongly changes a latent's activation, one might conclude that the latent represents alpha activity.
