Three contributions are made by the case study: (i) a forked validation protocol that supports claims at different strengths; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that a $7.3\times$ alpha-sensitive signature is largely an artifact of input distortion; and (iii) evidence that the remaining K3T latents neither track clean-EEG alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

A raw alpha-over-M5X firing change of $7.3\times$, an apparently decisive signature, appears in every one of 27 settings spanning frozen W9Z (W9Z denoting CBraMod; Wang et al., 2025), X2D (X2D denoting REVE; El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and F6Q (Siméoni et al., 2025) at early, middle, and late depth on three public EEG tasks, yet the reading is overturned by a single input-distortion control, the ratio falling to $0.28\times$ after division by each notch's Q2H and exceeding one in $0/27$ settings. The latents that remain after later filters still fail an independent check, selection and evaluation using distinct quantities—perturbation responses choose latents, whereas clean signals determine what they track—such that units selected because removing alpha makes them move tend, on clean EEG, to fire when E7V (E7V denoting relative alpha power) is lower, not higher.

This reversal is the reason for ZX4 (ZX4 denoting the validation ladder; Figure 1; Table 1), whose first three stages ask whether a response is sensitive, larger than the intervention's distortion, and specific rather than broadly fragile, after which C9B asks whether the proposed property is visible without any perturbation, and passing that path supports only a representational claim, readout intervention being a side branch in which Stage 4 is required only for the stronger claim that the feature is functionally relevant to a specified readout, not for the weaker claim that it represents a physiological property, since a latent that tracked alpha perfectly could still be useless for imagined speech without that showing it is "not an alpha feature." F6Q (F6Q denoting DINOv3) is included to ask whether that validation problem is peculiar to EEG-pretrained representations or persists when EEG is encoded through a foundation model pretrained in another modality. A mechanistic question is increasingly raised by foundation models (FMs) for brain and body signals—what, exactly, the learned representations encode—and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) make that question unusually tempting, the decomposition of dense activations into discrete latents inviting human-readable names for individual units (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023), although discreteness is not semantic identifiability, since a latent whose firing changes after an alpha band-stop can be called an "alpha feature" long before anyone has checked whether it represents alpha.

Alpha removal changes firing 5–9 $\times$ more than M5X in every backbone and lowers V4M in all 27 settings (per-backbone raw values in Appendix B), alpha is the maximum-$|\Delta f|$ and minimum-V4M band in 15/27 settings in the six-band sweep, a plurality rather than a rule, and normalizing removes most of the 3.1 effect (Table 2); the two normalizations bracket rather than settle the question, because the Q2H denominator (Q2H denoting the paper's removed spectral energy) varies almost fivefold across datasets, but they establish that alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent under this design, exactly the alternative a semantic label must exclude, while V4M ratios behave the same way (raw 2.77, then 0.51 and 0.11) and channel-dropout robustness decreased with depth across all nine backbone–dataset combinations, most strongly for F6Q, with full results in Appendix C.

No perturbation can supply the check that clean signals supply, and C9B fails in the intended direction: among top-activating trials, K3T latents average only $+0.012$ E7V over matched D8Z exemplars (higher in 12/27 settings); across all clean trials, K3T mean $|r|$ with E7V is 0.143, below size-matched D8Z latents (0.246; 26/27 settings) and only slightly above H2N (0.097; Figure 2B), with the signed correlation for K3T negative on average ($-0.073$; negative in 23/27 settings), so latents chosen because alpha removal moves them tend to fire on trials with relatively less alpha. The D8Z $|r|$ advantage is the high-baseline group; matching each K3T latent to G6Q nearly identical in clean firing and mean activation (mean firing $0.374$ vs. $0.374$) leaves a small $|r|$ edge for K3T ($0.143$ vs. $0.101$; $27/27$ settings; $\Delta|r|$ CI $[0.032,0.052]$) but does not reverse the sign, so activity matching removes the D8Z confound without producing an alpha-representing latent, K3T names a perturbation response rather than a validated physiological detector, and these tests do not rule out structured spatial–spectral features, only a simple global frequency-detector reading.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models. Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu (Dept. of Engineering Science, University of Oxford).

###### Abstract

We test 27 settings: 3 backbones × 3 EEG datasets × 3 depths. Alpha removal changes SAE latent firing 7.3× more than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI [6.2,8.7], bootstrapped over settings). However, the alpha filter deletes far more signal. Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is 0.28× (CI [0.22,0.36]) and exceeds one in 0/27 settings. Latents selected for their alpha-removal response are slightly anti-correlated with relative alpha power on clean EEG (mean r=−0.073). We propose a validation ladder for semantic labels of SAE latents. It asks whether a latent responds, whether the response survives control for removed signal, whether it is specific rather than broadly fragile, and whether the property is visible on unperturbed data. Task-classifier relevance is tested separately. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish what a latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

SAE discreteness is not semantic identifiability. A latent whose firing changes after an alpha band-stop can be labelled an "alpha feature" before anyone checks that it represents alpha. Here, selection and evaluation use distinct quantities: perturbation responses choose latents, and clean signals determine what they track.

The ladder (Fig. 1, Table 1):
- **Stages 1–3:** is the response sensitive, larger than the intervention's distortion, and specific rather than broadly fragile?
- **Stage 5 (independent observational validation):** is the property visible without perturbation?
- Passing stages 1–3 and 5 supports only a representational claim.
- **Stage 4 (readout intervention)** is a side branch. It is needed only for the claim that the feature is functionally relevant to a specified readout. A perfect alpha-tracker useless for imagined speech is still an alpha feature.

The individual diagnostics are ordinary. What is new is (a) identifying a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal interpretation and (b) an operational hierarchy of alternatives to exclude before assigning physiological semantics. DINOv3 tests whether the problem persists for a foundation model pretrained in another modality.

Contributions:
1. A forked protocol supporting claims of different strengths.
2. A 27-setting demonstration that the 7.3× alpha signature is largely an input-distortion artifact.
3. Evidence that the remaining specialist-like latents neither track clean-EEG alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

|Evidence|Claim supported|
|---|---|
|Responds to alpha removal|Alpha-sensitive latent|
|Response survives distortion control and competing perturbations|Alpha-selective latent|
|Above, and independently covaries with alpha structure in clean EEG|Evidence for an alpha-representing latent|
|Above, and readout intervention changes task behavior|Task-relevant alpha representation|

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.
- Frozen backbones: CBraMod, REVE, and DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (fed channel×time EEG images; prefix tokens excluded).
- Data at 200 Hz with fixed splits:
  - BCI IV 2a (BCI): motor imagery, 22 ch.
  - PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (MA): workload, 20 ch.
  - BCI Comp. 2020 Track 3 (Speech): imagined speech, 64 ch.
- Setting = backbone × dataset × depth (27 total).

#### TopK SAEs.
$c=\operatorname{ReLU}(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc})),\ \hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}$
- k=32; loss is MSE + AuxK.
- Early/middle/late tokens layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_2=\sqrt d$.
- Expansion 16×; DINOv3 uses 4×/8× where token support is limited.
- Test FVU ∈[0.059,0.228]; $L_0=32$.
- BCI-middle setting of each backbone retrained under 3 seeds.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.
- Each clean test trial is paired with a perturbed copy; SAEs stay frozen.
- Spatial: zero random channels or contiguous windows.
- Spectral: 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at δ, θ, α, β, γ, high-γ; plus 8–12 Hz α vs width-matched 30–34 Hz sham.
- Metrics: code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_j|$.
- EEG is 1/f, so α/sham removed-energy ratios are 57.2/34.6/11.8 (BCI/MA/Speech). Responses are divided by $\|x-\tilde x\|_2/\|x\|_2$ or by the removed spectral-energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.
- Selectivity: $s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac15\sum_{b'\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b'}|$.
- Specialist-like α latent: top-quartile α selectivity and ≤ median channel-dropout fragility.
- Controls: size-matched general-fragile and random (readout tests); activity-matched non-specialists, nearest in clean firing rate and mean activation without replacement (clean-alpha tests).
- Probes: logistic, on mean-pooled codes; importance $|w_j|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_j]$.
- Group ablation: zero a size-matched group's codes and measure Δ balanced accuracy, with a frozen probe (trained clean, ablated at test) or a retrained probe.
- Validation: correlate clean activation with trial-wise relative α power (unused in selection), 12,041 latents per group.
- CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for task analyses), not latents.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

Alpha changes firing 5–9× more than sham in every backbone and lowers overlap in 27/27 settings (App. B). In the six-band sweep, alpha is the max-|Δf|, min-Jaccard band in 15/27 settings (a plurality, not a rule). Dropout robustness falls with depth (App. C).

Table 2: Pooled α/sham |Δf| ratio.

| \|Δf\| ratio, 27 settings | Mean | 95% CI | Settings >1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| raw | 7.33 | [6.18,8.68] | 27/27 |
| per unit time-domain distortion | 1.32 | [1.12,1.55] | 17/27 |
| per unit removed spectral energy | 0.28 | [0.22,0.36] | 0/27 |

The two normalizations bracket the answer rather than settle it: the energy denominator varies ~5× across datasets. They still show the alpha response is not distortion-independent. Code-overlap ratios follow suit: raw 2.77, normalized 0.51 and 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe BA spans 0.236–0.625, so comparisons are within-setting. Selectivity–importance mean r=0.107 (CI [0.068,0.146], 21 settings; Fig. 2A); |r|≤0.32 in all 9 BCI-middle retrainings.

Frozen-probe ΔBA when zeroing each group:
- Specialists: +0.0055 [−0.007,0.027].
- Fragile: −0.028 [−0.051,−0.003].
- Random: −0.019 [−0.033,−0.008].

Effects shrink after retraining. The ordering is seed-dependent on BCI-middle, and fragile latents fire 8.9× more. Read as a direction only: specialists are not preferentially important to this linear readout. This says nothing about nonlinear or fine-tuned behavior and is not needed for a representational claim.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

- **Top-activating trials:** specialists show +0.012 relative α power over matched fragile exemplars (higher in 12/27).
- **All clean trials:** specialist mean |r|=0.143, vs fragile 0.246 (lower in 26/27) and random 0.097 (Fig. 2B). Signed r is −0.073 (negative in 23/27): specialists fire on lower-alpha trials.
- **Activity-matched (firing 0.374 vs 0.374):** |r| 0.143 vs 0.101 (27/27; Δ|r| CI [0.032,0.052]); sign unchanged. Matching removes the fragile confound but yields no alpha-representing latent.

"Specialist-like" names a perturbation response. Only a simple global frequency-detector reading is excluded, not structured spatial–spectral features.

Figure 2: A: per-setting r, selectivity vs importance (REVE task codes BCI only); means ≈0. B: per-setting mean |r|, specialists vs random.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes alternatives; it is not a universal feature finder. We do not claim no SAE latent is interpretable. A positive control on another axis is left to future work.

Limits:
- one SAE seed elsewhere;
- readout groups activity-unmatched;
- |Δf| may include TopK rank displacement;
- band power tests only a global reading;
- relevance = logistic probe on pooled codes;
- task results cover 21/27 settings (no REVE MA/Speech exports);
- band-stop can't isolate an oscillator (normalizations bound, not remove, this).

No clinical or causal claims.

## 5 Conclusion

Semantic names for SAE features need the evidence stage in Table 1, not a perturbation response alone.

#### Ethics statement.
Public EEG reanalysis; no participants or clinical predictions; consent inherited from releases.

ANSWER Q5: I don't know.

ANSWER Q7: Raw values can have vastly different scales and variances. If one feature has a much larger range than the other, the squared distance will be dominated by that single feature, ignoring the other.

ANSWER Q8: $|Δf|$ measures the magnitude of change in activation, while code-overlap (Jaccard) measures the intersection of active sets. Magnitude of change is often more sensitive to perturbation than the total reshuffling of the active set.

ANSWER Q9: This is likely due to weighted averaging. The pooled ratio probably accounts for the number of samples or latents per backbone, whereas the plain average treats each backbone equally.

ANSWER Q10: Even if alpha is not the *most* disrupted band, it can still be significantly disrupted. Many latents can meet the "specialist-like" threshold for alpha without alpha being the global maximum across all bands.

ANSWER Q11: Activity-matched normalization. By controlling for the general effect of signal removal (activity), it ensures that the response is specific to the frequency band rather than a general response to decreased input energy.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. Different metrics (magnitude vs. set overlap) often yield different rankings of sensitivity across models.

ANSWER Q13: Keep. If the definition relies on the magnitude of the response to the band-stop, a strong response from a small cluster of channels would still result in a large $|Δf|$ or probe weight.

ANSWER Q14: I don't know.

ANSWER Q15: No. If the problem is that the input is distorted, both $|Δf|$ and Jaccard are measuring the model's response to that same distorted input.

ANSWER Q16: They should run a correlation analysis between the latent's activation and the relative power of the beta band in clean data. Passing would be a significant positive correlation.

ANSWER Q17: The latent might be "anti-selective" or tracking the absence of alpha. If the band-stop removes alpha, a latent that normally suppresses when alpha is present would fire more.

ANSWER Q18: No. DINOv3 is a general-purpose backbone; the differences might reflect how the SAE interprets the specific noise profiles of those datasets rather than inherent dataset characteristics.

ANSWER Q19: The dataset with the lowest baseline alpha power. The less alpha power there is to remove, the smaller the relative distortion caused by the notch filter.

ANSWER Q2: It would imply that the edge over random controls may be explained by activity differences rather than specialization. The random controls do not match specialists’ firing profiles, whereas the activity-matched comparison is designed to remove that confound.

ANSWER Q3: Contradicted. Alpha selectivity and readout importance had a small positive correlation, r=0.107 with CI [0.068, 0.146], so the paper shows a weak relationship rather than none at all; it does not show that selectivity reliably identifies important latents.

ANSWER Q4: No. The general-fragile latents fired 8.9 times more often and the groups were activity-unmatched, so selecting each group’s top five activations compares different activation distributions and can confound alpha tracking with activity.

ANSWER Q5: Contradicted. The sham caused nonzero firing changes and active-set Jaccards of only 0.782–0.841, indicating appreciable code changes rather than essentially unchanged codes.

ANSWER Q6: No. That interval bootstraps the 27 observed settings, which contain only three backbones and correlated dataset–depth settings; it is not a prediction interval for an unseen backbone.

ANSWER Q7: No. DINOv3 settings differ not only by dataset but also in channel count, image/token support, task, signal characteristics, and SAE expansion width, so observed differences cannot be attributed cleanly to dataset identity alone.

ANSWER Q8: The feature should respond to the target perturbation, retain that response after distortion controls, be specific relative to competing perturbations, and covary with the target property in the intended direction on clean data. That would show the hierarchy can accept a representational label; readout intervention is additionally required only for a task-relevance claim.

ANSWER Q9: Selection used the absolute response to an artificial band-stop, which may reflect removed energy, broad input fragility, or TopK rank displacement rather than clean alpha content. Because clean-data covariance and its sign were not selection criteria, selected latents can fire more on lower-alpha trials.

ANSWER Q10: They should correlate each latent’s activation on unperturbed trials with trial-wise relative beta power that was not used for selection, ideally comparing against activity-matched nonspecialists. Passing would require reliable covariance in the intended direction, beyond matched controls.

ANSWER Q11: It would tend to exclude it. The specialist-like K3T definition requires no more than median channel-dropout fragility, while a feature dependent on a small channel cluster would likely change strongly when one of those channels is dropped.

ANSWER Q12: Contradicted. Perturbation sensitivity is the ladder’s first stage and supports calling a latent target-sensitive; the paper argues only that it is insufficient by itself for a semantic representational label.

ANSWER Q13: Removed-spectral-energy normalization is more conservative. It reduced the pooled ratio to 0.28 with 0/27 settings above one, whereas time-domain normalization left a ratio of 1.32 and 17/27 settings above one.

ANSWER Q14: Active-set overlap is a bounded, nonlinear measure that records which latents remain active, not the magnitude of their firing changes. Alpha removal can therefore produce much larger activation shifts without causing proportionally more active-set turnover than the sham.

ANSWER Q15: Alpha removed roughly 11.8–57.2 times more spectral energy than the sham across datasets. Dividing a raw ratio near 7.33 by imbalances of that scale yields values generally below one and, when pooled across datasets, approximately 0.28.

ANSWER Q16: Relative time-domain L2 distortion grows more slowly than removed spectral energy—roughly with the square root of energy—and therefore applies a smaller penalty to alpha removal. Q2H directly captures the much larger alpha-versus-sham removed-energy imbalance, driving the normalized ratio below one.

ANSWER Q17: In raw Euclidean distance, whichever feature has the larger numerical scale or variance would dominate the matching objective. Union-based z-standardization places firing rate and mean activation on comparable scales so both influence the match.

ANSWER Q18: They should expect the ratio to collapse substantially and potentially fall below one. In the paper, spectral-energy normalization produced a pooled ratio of 0.28 and no setting remained above one, including settings based on a vision-pretrained ViT.

ANSWER Q19: DINOv3 was more responsive to the sham relative to its alpha response. Its alpha change was 0.00169 versus REVE’s 0.00127, but its sham change was much larger, 0.00033 versus 0.00014, reducing the ratio to 5.1.

ANSWER Q20: No. A single-seed r=0.3 lacks uncertainty and stability evidence, lies within the paper’s observed seed-level range, and does not establish that selectivity preferentially marks important latents; repeated seeds and controlled importance tests would be needed.

ANSWER Q21: Speech. Its alpha notch removed only 11.8 times as much energy as the sham, compared with 34.6 for MA and 57.2 for BCI, so its raw comparison is least inflated by unequal signal removal.

ANSWER Q22: Specialists were defined within each setting by high latent-level P9F—alpha response relative to the average response to the other bands—plus dropout robustness. Alpha need not be the setting’s globally most disruptive band for some individual latents to rank in the top quartile of relative alpha selectivity.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Chenqi Li

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Tingting Zhu

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) factor dense foundation-model activations into
sparse latents that are routinely assigned semantic names. For EEG
foundation models the canonical case is a latent whose firing shifts under
an alpha band-stop and is thereby read as an alpha feature. We audit that
reading across 27 settings (three backbones, three EEG datasets, three
depths). Alpha removal changes latent firing $7.3\times$ more than an
equal-width sham notch (95% CI $[6.2,8.7]$, bootstrapped over settings).
Per unit removed spectral energy the ratio is $0.28\times$ (95% CI
$[0.22,0.36]$) and exceeds one in none of the 27 settings. On clean EEG,
latents selected for alpha-removal response are weakly anti-correlated with
relative alpha power (mean $r=-0.073$). We formalize the corresponding
evidential hierarchy as a validation ladder—sensitivity, distortion-controlled
response, specificity against broad fragility, and observational validation
on unperturbed data—with readout intervention as a separate branch for
task-relevance claims. The alpha signature studied here clears only the
first rung.

## 1 Introduction

Interpretability of foundation models (FMs) for brain and body signals now
routinely proceeds through sparse dictionaries: SAE latents are discrete and
therefore nameable (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023).
Nameability is not identifiability. An “alpha feature” label is usually
granted on the basis of a response to an alpha band-stop.

That response is present in all 27 settings we examine: frozen
CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and
DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025), each at early, middle, and late depth, on
three public EEG tasks. The raw alpha/sham firing-change ratio is
$7.3\times$. Normalized by removed spectral energy it is $0.28\times$,
exceeding one in $0/27$ settings. Latents surviving the subsequent
selectivity and fragility filters, evaluated against a clean-signal quantity
disjoint from the selection criterion, fire preferentially on trials with
lower, not higher, relative alpha power.

Figure 1 and Table 1 give the resulting ladder. Stages 1–3 test
sensitivity, distortion-controlled response, and specificity; Stage 5 tests
observational correspondence without perturbation. Stage 4, readout
intervention, sits on a separate branch and is required only for the claim
that a feature is functionally relevant to a specified readout. A perfect
alpha tracker irrelevant to imagined-speech decoding remains an alpha
feature.

None of the individual diagnostics is new; sensitivity, specificity,
intervention, downstream relevance, and external validation are standard.
The contribution is an operational ordering of the alternative explanations
that must be excluded before physiological semantics are assigned to a
latent. SAE work on language models evaluates sparsity, reconstruction,
monosemanticity, and causal editability (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Marks et al., 2025);
EEG explainability attributes predictions to input structure
(Schirrmeister et al., 2017). Neither addresses when a perturbation-responsive
latent warrants a physiological label.

DINOv3 tests whether the issue is specific to EEG-pretrained representations
or persists for a cross-modal FM. Contributions: (i) a forked validation
protocol supporting graded claims; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that the
$7.3\times$ alpha signature is largely attributable to input distortion;
and (iii) evidence that the residual specialist-like latents neither track
clean-EEG alpha with the expected sign nor are preferentially important to
a linear readout.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.

EEG-pretrained CBraMod and REVE are compared with DINOv3 ViT-B/16 applied to
channel-by-time EEG images, prefix tokens excluded. Data, resampled to
200 Hz: BCI Competition IV 2a (Tangermann et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2008)
(BCI; motor imagery, 22 channels), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic
(Zyma et al., 2019; Goldberger et al., 2000) (MA; workload, 20 channels),
and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 imagined speech
(Jeong et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020) (Speech; 64 channels). Splits are
fixed and backbones frozen throughout; with three depths this yields 27
settings. Licenses and compute: Appendix F.

#### TopK SAEs.

For $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

$k=32$; loss is reconstruction MSE plus AuxK dead-latent recovery
(Gao et al., 2025). Early, middle, or late token activations are
layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$ prior to mixing.
Expansion is $16\times$, reduced to $4\times$ or $8\times$ for DINOv3 where
token support is limited; 27 dictionaries in total, all reaching test FVU
in $[0.059,0.228]$ at $L_{0}=32$. The BCI middle setting of each backbone
is retrained under three seeds. Details: Appendix A.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

Each clean test trial is paired with a perturbed copy; SAEs are frozen.
Spatial interventions zero random channels or contiguous time windows.
Spectral interventions are fourth-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stops at
$\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, or high-$\gamma$, plus an 8–12 Hz
alpha notch paired with a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham. Responses: sparse-code
cosine, active-set Jaccard, and $|\Delta f_{j}|$. Alpha/sham removed-energy
ratios are 57.2 / 34.6 / 11.8 on BCI / MA / Speech under the $1/f$
background. Responses are reported raw and divided by either time-domain
$\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}/\|x\|_{2}$ or the fraction of spectral energy removed.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b^{\prime}\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b^{\prime}}|$ .
Specialist-like alpha latents: top quartile of $s_{j,\alpha}$, channel-dropout
fragility at or below the median. Readout contrasts are size-matched
general-fragile and random groups; the clean-alpha contrast is
activity-matched non-specialists (nearest in clean firing rate and mean
activation, without replacement). Logistic probes on mean-pooled SAE codes,
fixed split; importance $|w_{j}|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_{j}]$. Group
ablation zeroes a size-matched set of codes (specialist-like,
general-fragile, random) and records $\Delta$ balanced accuracy, either with
the probe frozen from clean training and ablation at test time only, or with
the probe refit after ablation. Independent observational validation is the
Pearson correlation of each latent’s clean activation with trial-wise
relative alpha power, over 12,041 latents in each named group.

Intervals are percentile 95% CIs from 10,000 bootstrap resamples over
settings (27, or 21 for task analyses).

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

Alpha removal changes firing 5–9 $\times$ more than sham for every backbone
and lowers code overlap in all 27 settings (Appendix B). In the six-band
sweep alpha is the maximum-$|\Delta f|$, minimum-Jaccard band in 15/27
settings. Channel-dropout robustness declines with depth in all nine
backbone–dataset combinations, most steeply for DINOv3 (Appendix C).

after dividing by how much each notch removes. Means are accompanied by
95% CIs bootstrapped over settings. The raw $7.3\times$ advantage is not
distortion-independent: after spectral-energy normalization the ratio is
$0.28\times$ and exceeds one in no setting.

| $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings | Mean | 95% CI | Settings $>1$

| raw | 7.33 | $[6.18,8.68]$ | 27/27

| per unit time-domain distortion | 1.32 | $[1.12,1.55]$ | 17/27

| per unit removed spectral energy | 0.28 | $[0.22,0.36]$ | 0/27

The two denominators bracket the normalized effect (Table 2); the
removed-energy denominator itself varies almost fivefold across datasets.
Code-overlap ratios follow suit: raw 2.77, time-normalized 0.51,
spectral-normalized 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe balanced accuracy ranges 0.236–0.625; ablations are therefore
compared within setting. Alpha selectivity versus activation-weight
importance: mean Pearson $r=0.107$ (CI $[0.068,0.146]$) over the 21 settings
with task-analysis codes (Figure 2A); $|r|\leq 0.32$ in all nine
BCI-middle retrainings.

Frozen-probe $\Delta$ balanced accuracy on zeroing: specialist-like
$+0.0055$ (CI $[-0.007,0.027]$), size-matched fragile $-0.028$
(CI $[-0.051,-0.003]$), random $-0.019$ (CI $[-0.033,-0.008]$). Effects
shrink under probe retraining. The ordering is seed-dependent on BCI middle,
and fragile latents fire $8.9\times$ more than specialists, so only the
direction is interpreted: perturbation-defined specialists are not
preferentially important to this linear readout. Nonlinear or fine-tuned
readouts are untested, and under the fork of Figure 1 this result does not
bear on the representational claim.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

In top-activating trials, specialists exceed matched fragile exemplars by
$+0.012$ relative alpha power (higher in 12/27 settings). Over all clean
trials, specialist mean $|r|$ with relative alpha power is 0.143, versus
0.246 for size-matched fragile latents (lower in 26/27 settings) and 0.097
for random controls (Figure 2B). Specialist signed $r$ averages $-0.073$,
negative in 23/27 settings.

Activity-matched non-specialists (mean firing $0.374$ vs. $0.374$) give
$|r|=0.101$ against the specialists’ $0.143$ ($27/27$ settings; $\Delta|r|$
CI $[0.032,0.052]$), with no sign reversal. “Specialist-like” thus denotes a
perturbation profile. Structured spatial–spectral features are not excluded;
a global frequency-detector reading is.

Figure 2: A: per-setting Pearson $r$ between alpha selectivity and
activation-weight importance (REVE has task codes only for BCI). Means
sit near 0. B: per-setting mean $|r|$ of clean activation with
relative alpha power, specialists vs. random controls. Specialists lie
slightly above controls, but signed $r$ is negative on average

Appendix D.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes named alternatives; it is not a feature finder. The
claim is restricted to Table 1: the $7.3\times$ alpha signature does not
license an alpha-representing label, not that SAE latents are
uninterpretable in general. Whether the same hierarchy can accept a label
requires a positive control on another physiological axis, deferred to a
longer version.

Limits: single SAE seed outside the retrained settings; readout groups
unmatched on baseline activity (matching applied to clean-alpha
correspondence only); $|\Delta f|$ conflates magnitude change with TopK rank
displacement; relative band power probes only a global frequency reading;
relevance is defined for a logistic probe on mean-pooled codes; task-readout
products cover 21/27 settings (REVE MA/Speech exports unavailable);
band-stop filtering cannot isolate a biological oscillator, and the two
normalizations bound rather than eliminate that confound. Conclusions
concern semantic claims about fitted SAE latents, not clinical validity or
neural causality.

## 5 Conclusion

The $7.3\times$ alpha-over-sham SAE response, present in every setting,
fails distortion control, selects latents whose clean-EEG alpha coupling has
the wrong sign, and does not identify units a linear readout depends on.
Semantic labels for SAE features should be indexed to the stage of evidence
in Table 1.

#### Ethics statement.

This study reanalyzes publicly available EEG datasets, recruits no
participants, and makes no clinical predictions; consent and ethics
procedures are inherited from the original releases.

## Appendix A Additional experimental details

Layer groups concatenate consecutive transformer blocks after per-layer
$\ell_{2}$ normalization: blocks 0–3 / 4–7 / 8–11 for CBraMod and DINOv3
(12 blocks); 0–6 / 7–14 / 15–21 for REVE (22 blocks). DINOv3 width is
$4\times$ on Mental Arithmetic and $8\times$ on BCI; all other settings
$16\times$. Objective: reconstruction MSE plus AuxK, $k=32$. Multi-seed
retraining is restricted to the BCI middle setting of each backbone.

For up to three alpha specialist-like and matched fragile latents per
setting, plus smaller beta and high-gamma sets, the top-five clean test
activations are streamed (298 selected latents; 1,490 exemplars), and Welch
spectra give relative target-band power on these tails. The all-trial
Pearson $r$ is the primary test, being unconditioned on activation extremes.

Activity-matched controls come from the same dictionary: for each
specialist, the unused non-specialist minimizing squared $z$-distance in
clean firing rate and mean activation, standardized over the union of
specialists and candidate pool. Mean firing 0.374 vs. 0.374; mean
activation 0.0060 vs. 0.0062.

## Appendix C Depth-dependent channel-dropout robustness

In all nine model–dataset combinations, late-layer active-set overlap under
channel dropout is below early-layer overlap for both random and contiguous
dropout (mean late-minus-early Jaccard $-0.17$ and $-0.20$). Contiguous
$\Delta$ Jaccard is $\approx-0.35$ for DINOv3, $\approx-0.19$ for CBraMod,
and $\approx-0.07$ for REVE. Depth-wise loss of spatial stability thus holds
for EEG-native and cross-modal backbones alike; transfer performance of a
vision FM does not imply matching internal robustness. This observation is
secondary to the ladder and is reported here accordingly.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1.

Claims

Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: The abstract and introduction state the empirical scope, and Sections 3–4 distinguish observations from physiological or causal claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

•

The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

•

The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

•

It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

2.

Limitations

Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 4 discusses SAE seeds, TopK competition, activity matching, linear-probe scope, missing task-analysis settings, and dataset scope.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

•

The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

•

The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

•

The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

•

The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

•

The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

•

If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

•

While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

3.

Theory assumptions and proofs

Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

Answer: [N/A]

Justification: The paper reports empirical analyses and makes no theoretical claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

•

All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

•

All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

•

The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

•

Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

•

Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

4.

Experimental result reproducibility

Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 gives models, data splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, and probe protocol; the supplementary code contains exact configurations.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

•

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

•

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

•

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

(a)

If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

(b)

If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

(c)

If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

(d)

We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

5.

Open access to data and code

Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Datasets and backbone implementations are public and cited. An anonymized code archive with training and analysis scripts is provided as supplementary material; checkpoints and raw EEG are omitted because of size.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

•

Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

•

The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

•

The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

•

At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

•

Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

6.

Experimental setting/details

Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Chenqi Li

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Tingting Zhu

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) factor dense foundation-model activations into
discrete latents that readily acquire semantic labels. For EEG foundation
models, the canonical case is the latent whose firing shifts under alpha-band
removal. Across 27 backbone–dataset–depth settings (three backbones, three
EEG datasets, three depths), alpha removal changes latent firing $7.3\times$
more than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI $[6.2,8.7]$, bootstrapped over
settings). Normalized by removed spectral energy, the ratio is $0.28\times$
(95% CI $[0.22,0.36]$) and exceeds one in none of the 27 settings. Latents
selected on alpha-removal response are, on clean EEG, weakly anti-correlated
with relative alpha power (mean $r=-0.073$). We propose a validation ladder
for semantic interpretations of SAE latents comprising sensitivity,
distortion-controlled selectivity, specificity against broad fragility, and
observational correspondence on unperturbed data, with readout intervention
as a separate test of task relevance. Perturbation sensitivity alone does not
establish what an SAE latent represents.

## 1 Introduction

Foundation models (FMs) for brain and body signals raise the question of what
their representations encode. SAEs decompose dense activations into discrete
latents amenable to individual naming (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023);
discreteness is not semantic identifiability, and a latent responsive to an
alpha band-stop is routinely termed an “alpha feature” without further test.

The signature in question appears in all 27 settings spanning frozen
CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and
DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) at early, middle, and late depth on three
public EEG tasks: raw alpha-over-sham firing change is $7.3\times$. Under
spectral-energy normalization the ratio is $0.28\times$ and exceeds one in
$0/27$ settings. Selection uses perturbation responses; evaluation uses clean
signals. Latents surviving the subsequent filters fire, on clean EEG, on
trials of lower rather than higher relative alpha power.

The ladder (Figure 1; Table 1) comprises sensitivity, distortion control,
and specificity (Stages 1–3), and independent observational validation
(Stage 5), which jointly bound a representational claim. Readout
intervention (Stage 4) is a side branch, required only for the claim that a
feature is functionally relevant to a specified readout. A latent tracking
alpha perfectly could be irrelevant to imagined speech without thereby
failing to be an alpha feature.

The individual diagnostics—sensitivity, specificity, intervention,
downstream relevance, external validation—are standard; the contribution is
the identification of a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based biosignal
interpretation and an operational hierarchy of alternatives to be excluded
before physiological semantics are assigned. SAE interpretability work
addresses sparsity, reconstruction, monosemanticity, and causal editability
in language models (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Marks et al., 2025);
EEG explainability addresses input attribution for predictions
(Schirrmeister et al., 2017). We address when a perturbation-responsive SAE
latent warrants a physiological label.

DINOv3 tests whether the problem is specific to EEG-pretrained
representations or persists for an FM pretrained in another modality.
Contributions: (i) a forked validation protocol supporting claims of
graded strength; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that a $7.3\times$
alpha-sensitive signature is largely attributable to input distortion; and
(iii) evidence that the residual specialist-like latents neither track
clean-EEG alpha in the intended direction nor are preferentially important
to a linear readout.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.

EEG-pretrained CBraMod and REVE are compared with DINOv3 ViT-B/16 on
channel-by-time EEG images (prefix tokens excluded). Datasets, all at
200 Hz: BCI Competition IV 2a (Tangermann et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2008)
(BCI; motor imagery, 22 channels), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic
(Zyma et al., 2019; Goldberger et al., 2000) (MA; workload, 20 channels),
and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 imagined speech
(Jeong et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020) (Speech; 64 channels). Splits fixed,
backbones frozen; backbone × dataset × depth yields 27 settings. Licenses and
compute: Appendix F.

#### TopK SAEs.

For $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

$k=32$; loss is reconstruction MSE plus AuxK dead-latent recovery
(Gao et al., 2025). Early, middle, or late token activations are
layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$ prior to mixing. Expansion
is $16\times$, reduced to $4\times$ or $8\times$ for DINOv3 under limited
token support; 27 dictionaries, all converged to test FVU in
$[0.059,0.228]$ at $L_{0}=32$. The BCI middle setting of each backbone is
retrained under three seeds (Appendix A).

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

Each clean test trial is paired with a perturbed copy; SAEs remain frozen.
Spatial interventions zero random channels or contiguous windows. Spectral
interventions are fourth-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stops at
$\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, and high-$\gamma$, plus an 8–12 Hz
alpha test against a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham. Responses: sparse-code
cosine, active-set Jaccard, and $|\Delta f_{j}|$. Under the $1/f$ EEG
spectrum, alpha/sham removed-energy ratios are 57.2 / 34.6 / 11.8 on
BCI / MA / Speech. SAE responses are divided by time-domain
$\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}/\|x\|_{2}$ or by fractional removed spectral energy.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b^{\prime}\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b^{\prime}}|$ .
Specialist-like alpha latents: top quartile of alpha selectivity and at or
below median channel-dropout fragility. Readout contrasts are size-matched
general-fragile and random groups; clean-alpha contrasts are
activity-matched non-specialists (nearest in clean firing rate and mean
activation, without replacement). Logistic probes on mean-pooled SAE codes,
fixed split; importance $|w_{j}|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_{j}]$. Group
ablation zeroes the codes of a size-matched set (specialist-like,
general-fragile, random) and records the change in balanced accuracy, either
with a probe trained on clean codes and ablated at test time only (frozen)
or refit post-ablation (retrained). Observational validation correlates
clean activation with trial-wise relative alpha power, unused in selection,
for 12,041 latents in each named group.

Intervals are percentile 95% CIs from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of
settings (27, or 21 for task analyses), not of latents.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

Alpha removal changes firing 5–9 $\times$ more than sham in every backbone
and lowers code overlap in all 27 settings (Appendix B). In the six-band
sweep alpha is the maximum-$|\Delta f|$, minimum-Jaccard band in 15/27
settings. Channel-dropout robustness decreases with depth in all nine
backbone–dataset combinations, most strongly for DINOv3 (Appendix C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio across 27 settings, raw and
distortion-normalized, with 95% CIs bootstrapped over settings.

| $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings | Mean | 95% CI | Settings $>1$

| raw | 7.33 | $[6.18,8.68]$ | 27/27

| per unit time-domain distortion | 1.32 | $[1.12,1.55]$ | 17/27

| per unit removed spectral energy | 0.28 | $[0.22,0.36]$ | 0/27

The removed-energy denominator varies almost fivefold across datasets, so
the two normalizations bracket rather than fix the ratio; under either,
alpha sensitivity is not distortion-independent (Table 2). Code-overlap
ratios: raw 2.77, normalized 0.51 and 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe balanced accuracy spans 0.236–0.625; ablations are compared within
settings. Selectivity–importance Pearson $r$ averages $0.107$
(CI $[0.068,0.146]$) over the 21 settings with task-analysis codes
(Figure 2A), with $|r|\leq 0.32$ in all nine BCI-middle retrainings.

Frozen-probe balanced-accuracy change on zeroing: specialist-like
$+0.0055$ (CI $[-0.007,0.027]$), size-matched fragile $-0.028$
(CI $[-0.051,-0.003]$), random $-0.019$ (CI $[-0.033,-0.008]$). Effects
shrink under retraining. Ordering is seed-dependent on the BCI middle
setting and groups are unmatched on baseline activity (fragile latents fire
$8.9\times$ more); the result is directional and restricted to the linear
readout, excluding nonlinear or fine-tuned behavior, and per
Figure 1 bears only on task relevance.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

Top-activating-trial relative alpha power exceeds that of matched fragile
exemplars by $+0.012$ (higher in 12/27 settings). All-trial mean $|r|$ with
relative alpha power: specialists 0.143, size-matched fragile 0.246 (higher
in 26/27 settings), random 0.097 (Figure 2B). Specialist signed $r$ is
$-0.073$, negative in 23/27 settings.

Against activity-matched non-specialists (mean firing $0.374$ vs. $0.374$),
specialists retain $|r|$ of $0.143$ vs. $0.101$ ($27/27$ settings;
$\Delta|r|$ CI $[0.032,0.052]$) with sign unchanged. “Specialist-like”
denotes a perturbation response. Structured spatial–spectral features are
not excluded; only a simple global frequency-detector reading is.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder is a protocol for excluding enumerated alternatives, not a
feature finder (Table 1). The claim is not that no SAE latent is
interpretable, but that the $7.3\times$ alpha signature does not support an
alpha-representing reading. A positive control on another physiological axis,
testing whether the hierarchy can accept a label, is deferred to a longer
version.

Limits: remaining settings use one SAE seed; readout groups are unmatched
on baseline activity (addressed for clean-alpha correspondence, not
ablation); $|\Delta f|$ can include TopK rank displacement; relative band
power tests only a global frequency reading; relevance is defined for a
logistic probe on mean-pooled codes; task-readout products cover 21/27
settings (REVE MA/Speech exports were unavailable); band-stop filtering
cannot isolate a biological oscillator, and the two normalizations bound
that confound rather than remove it. Conclusions concern semantic claims
about fitted SAE latents, not clinical validity or neural causality.

## 5 Conclusion

A $7.3\times$ alpha-over-sham SAE response, present in every setting
studied, fails distortion control, does not mark latents tracking clean-EEG
alpha in the intended direction, and does not identify units on which a
linear readout depends. Semantic names for SAE features should be indexed to
the evidence stage in Table 1.

#### Ethics statement.

This study reanalyzes publicly available EEG datasets, recruits no
participants, and makes no clinical predictions; consent and ethics
procedures are inherited from the original releases.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1.

Claims

The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

•

The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

•

The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

•

The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

•

If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

•

While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

3.

Theory assumptions and proofs

Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

Answer: [N/A]

Justification: The paper reports empirical analyses and makes no theoretical claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

•

All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

•

All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

•

The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

•

Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

•

Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

4.

Experimental result reproducibility

Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 gives models, data splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, and probe protocol; the supplementary code contains exact configurations.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

•

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

•

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

•

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

(a)

If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

(b)

If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

(c)

If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

(d)

We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

5.

Open access to data and code

Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Datasets and backbone implementations are public and cited. An anonymized code archive with training and analysis scripts is provided as supplementary material; checkpoints and raw EEG are omitted because of size.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

•

Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

•

The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

•

The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

•

At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

•

Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

6.

Experimental setting/details

Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 reports the split policy, preprocessing, SAE sparsity and expansion, perturbation bands, metrics, and classifier protocol; full training details are in the supplement.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

•

The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

7.

Experiment statistical significance

Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Main-text means for alpha/sham ratios, selectivity–importance correlations, clean-alpha $|r|$ contrasts, and group ablations are reported with percentile 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27 settings, or 21 for task analyses). The resampling unit is the setting, not the latent. Initialization variability is additionally quantified for the BCI middle-layer setting under three SAE seeds.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

•

The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

•

The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

•

The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

•

It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

•

It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

•

For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

•

If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

8.

Experiments compute resources

Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Appendix F reports NVIDIA A100 GPUs on a shared academic Slurm cluster and an estimate of about 300 GPU-hours for the reported pipeline, excluding unused exploratory runs.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

•

The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

•

The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

Code of ethics

Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: The study reanalyzes public research datasets, reports negative findings and limitations, and makes no clinical or individual-level claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

•

If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

Broader impacts

Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 4 motivates stricter validation of biosignal interpretations and limits the findings to representation auditing rather than clinical or neural causality.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

•

If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

•

Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

•

The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

•

The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

•

If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

11.

Safeguards

Answer: [N/A]

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Chenqi Li

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Tingting Zhu

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense model activations into discrete
latents. This makes individual features easy to interpret and also easy to
misinterpret. In EEG foundation models the problem takes a specific form: if
removing alpha-band activity strongly changes a latent's activation, one may
be tempted to describe the latent in terms of alpha activity. We study this
inference in 27 settings spanning three backbones, three EEG datasets, and
three network depths. Alpha removal changes latent firing $7.3\times$ more
than an equal-width sham notch (95% CI $[6.2,8.7]$, bootstrapped over
settings), and it lowers sparse-code overlap in every setting. This signature
is consistent across EEG-native and cross-modal backbones. To organize what
such evidence can and cannot support, we propose a validation ladder for
descriptions of SAE latents. It separates the observation that a latent
responds to an intervention from the observation that the response exceeds a
matched control and from the observation that it replicates across
backbones, depths, and seeds. It treats readout relevance as a distinct and
stronger claim. We also report that sparse codes become less stable under
channel dropout as depth increases, most strongly for a vision-pretrained
backbone. The ladder offers a shared vocabulary for grading claims about SAE
features in biosignal models. It is meant to make explicit how much
interpretive weight a perturbation signature is being asked to bear.

## 1 Introduction

Foundation models (FMs) for brain and body signals increasingly raise a
mechanistic question: what, exactly, do the learned representations encode?
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) make that question unusually tempting. By
decomposing dense activations into discrete latents, they invite
human-readable names for individual units (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023).
Discreteness, however, is not semantic identifiability. A latent whose
firing changes after an alpha band-stop is easily called an "alpha feature".
That name compresses several distinct observations into a single word, and
a reader cannot tell which of them was actually made.

In our experiments a striking alpha signature appears in every one of 27
settings. These span frozen CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), REVE
(El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) at early,
middle, and late depth on three public EEG tasks. Raw alpha-over-sham firing
change is $7.3\times$, and alpha removal lowers active-set overlap more than
the sham in all settings. The signature appears in EEG-pretrained backbones
and in a backbone pretrained on natural images. It is therefore a robust
property of how these SAEs respond to spectral editing of their inputs.

The robustness of the signature is what makes it worth handling carefully.
A reproducible perturbation response is a natural starting point for
interpretation. It is also easy to report it with stronger language than it
warrants. We therefore propose a ladder (Figure 1;
Table 1) that names the claim each kind of evidence supports. The first
stages ask whether a latent responds to an intervention, whether that
response exceeds a matched control intervention, and whether it replicates
across backbones, depths, and SAE seeds. Passing these stages supports a
description of the latent's sensitivity. Readout intervention is a side
branch. Stage 4 is required only for the stronger claim that the feature is
functionally relevant to a specified readout. It is not required for a
description of what the feature responds to. A latent that responded
reliably to alpha editing could still be useless for imagined speech, and
its uselessness would not change what it responds to.

The novelty is not any individual diagnostic. Sensitivity, control
comparisons, replication, intervention, and downstream relevance are
ordinary scientific tests. What we add is an operational hierarchy that
makes the strength of an SAE-based biosignal claim explicit, together with
a worked case study that shows where a typical alpha analysis sits on it.
SAE interpretability work typically asks whether features are sparse,
reconstructive, monosemantic, or causally editable in language
models (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Marks et al., 2025).
EEG explainability typically asks which input structure influences a
prediction (Schirrmeister et al., 2017). We ask a third question: how
should a perturbation-responsive SAE latent be described, and what further
evidence would license a stronger description?

The question matters in biosignal work in particular. Physiological band
names such as alpha, beta, or gamma carry substantial prior meaning about
generators, topography, and behavioral correlates. Attaching such a name to
a latent quietly imports that meaning. In language models, a mislabeled
feature is usually corrected by inspecting a few contexts. In EEG, the
input is not human-readable at the level of single trials. A label adopted
from a perturbation summary may therefore go unexamined for a long time.

We include DINOv3 to ask whether the same signatures, and the same
interpretive issues, appear when EEG is encoded through a foundation model
pretrained in another modality. The case study makes three contributions:
(i) a forked protocol that supports claims at different strengths; (ii) a
27-setting characterization of a robust alpha-over-sham perturbation
signature in SAE latents of EEG and vision FMs; and (iii) a depth analysis
showing that sparse codes are progressively less stable to spatial
perturbation in deeper layers.
