## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.

We compare EEG-pretrained CBraMod and REVE with DINOv3 ViT-B/16, which
receives channel-by-time EEG images (prefix tokens excluded). Three public
classification sets are sampled at 200 Hz: BCI Competition IV
2a (Tangermann et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2008) (BCI; motor imagery, 22
channels), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (Zyma et al., 2019; Goldberger et al., 2000)
(MA; workload, 20 channels), and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 imagined
speech (Jeong et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020) (Speech; 64 channels).
Splits are fixed and backbones are frozen. We refer to each combination of
backbone, dataset, and depth as a setting, which gives 27 settings in
total. Licenses and compute are listed in Appendix F.

#### TopK SAEs.

For $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

We set $k=32$ and train with reconstruction MSE plus AuxK dead-latent
recovery (Gao et al., 2025). Token activations from early, middle, or late
blocks are layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$ before mixing.
Dictionary expansion is $16\times$, except where limited token support
motivates $4\times$ or $8\times$ for DINOv3. This gives 27 dictionaries.
All converge to test FVU in $[0.059,0.228]$ with $L_{0}=32$. The BCI middle
setting of each backbone is retrained under three seeds. Further training
details are in Appendix A.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

Each clean test trial is paired with a perturbed copy. Spatial
interventions zero random channels or contiguous windows. Spectral
interventions apply a fourth-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at
$\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, or high-$\gamma$. We also run an
8–12 Hz alpha test against a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham. The sham shares
the filter order, bandwidth, and edge behavior of the alpha notch. It
therefore controls for generic consequences of passing a trial through a
band-stop filter, such as phase handling at the boundaries and transient
ringing. SAEs stay frozen. We record sparse-code cosine, active-set
Jaccard, and $|\Delta f_{j}|$, the absolute change in each latent's
activation between clean and perturbed copies.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

Selectivity is
$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b^{\prime}\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b^{\prime}}|$.
It compares a latent's response to one band against its mean response to
the other five. A specialist-like alpha latent is in the top quartile of
alpha selectivity and at or below median channel-dropout fragility.
Size-matched general-fragile and random groups serve as contrasts.
Mean-pooled SAE codes feed logistic probes on the fixed split. Importance
is $|w_{j}|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_{j}]$. A group ablation sets the codes
of a selected set of latents to zero and measures the resulting change in
probe balanced accuracy. Groups are matched in size across the
specialist-like, general-fragile, and random-control conditions. In the
frozen-probe variant the probe is trained on clean codes and the
ablation is applied only at test time. In the retrained variant the
probe is refit after ablation. Independent validation of perturbation
signatures takes the form of replication. We ask whether the same
signature appears in each backbone, at each depth, on each dataset, and
under SAE retraining with different seeds.

Confidence intervals in the text are percentile 95% intervals from 10,000
bootstrap resamples of settings, not of individual latents.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

Alpha removal changes firing 5–9$\times$ more than sham in every backbone
and lowers code overlap in all 27 settings (per-backbone values in
Table 2 and Appendix B). The pooled ratio is $7.33$ (CI $[6.18,8.68]$) and
exceeds one in 27/27 settings. The sham notch is the relevant
filter-matched control. It leaves sparse codes largely intact (mean sham
Jaccard between 0.78 and 0.84 across backbones), whereas the alpha notch
reduces mean Jaccard to roughly 0.47–0.54. Generic artifacts of applying a
zero-phase band-stop, if present, would affect both conditions alike.
What collapses, in other words, is code overlap, and only under the alpha
edit. Separately, channel-dropout robustness decreased with depth across
all nine backbone–dataset combinations, most strongly for DINOv3. Full
results are in Appendix C.

settings. The pooled interval is bootstrapped over settings.

| $|\Delta f|$ ratio | Mean | 95% CI | Settings $>1$

| REVE | 8.9 | – | 9/9

| DINOv3 | 5.1 | – | 9/9

| pooled, 27 settings | 7.33 | $[6.18,8.68]$ | 27/27

By the ladder's terms, this evidence establishes Stages 1–3 for a
sensitivity description. The latents respond to alpha removal. The
response exceeds a width-matched sham. The contrast replicates across all
three backbones, all three depths, and all three datasets. The appropriate
description is "robustly alpha-sensitive" at the population level. The
signature is notable for its consistency rather than its magnitude in any
single setting. The REVE ratio is the largest and the DINOv3 ratio the
smallest, yet all three sit well above one. Code-overlap contrasts point in
the same direction.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe balanced accuracy spans 0.236–0.625, so ablations are compared within
settings rather than pooled across them. Selectivity and importance are
different quantities by construction. Selectivity is computed from paired
clean and perturbed inputs and does not involve labels. Importance is
computed from a probe trained on clean codes and depends on the task. A
latent can be highly selective for a spectral edit while carrying
information that is redundant with other latents, or irrelevant to the
labeled contrast. Conversely, a latent important for motor imagery may
respond diffusely to every band-stop.

For this reason the ladder places readout intervention on a separate
branch. Group ablation with a frozen probe asks whether removing a
perturbation-defined group degrades a fixed decision rule. Retraining
after ablation asks whether the remaining code still contains the
information. These two variants answer different questions, and
retraining typically masks effects that are visible with a frozen readout.
The per-setting ablation display is given in Appendix D. Three properties
of the readout analysis limit how far it can be pushed. Groups differ in
baseline activity, since fragile latents fire $8.9\times$ more often than
specialist-like latents. The probes are linear on mean-pooled codes. The
analysis covers 21 settings. Readout relevance, whichever way it falls,
speaks to Stage 4 only. By the fork in Figure 1, it neither strengthens
nor weakens a sensitivity description established at Stages 1–3.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

Perturbation responses have a structural limitation. $|\Delta f_{j}|$ is
unsigned. A latent can move because alpha removal suppresses it or because
alpha removal releases it from competition under TopK sparsity. The
perturbation summary records only that the latent moved. Selectivity
inherits the same property. A specialist-like latent is one whose
magnitude of change is larger for alpha than for other bands, not one
whose activation rises with alpha content. In this sense the perturbation
evidence does not run in the direction an alpha-detector reading
intends. It does not say whether the latent fires more, less, or
differently when alpha is present.

Replication, the form of independent validation available in this design,
does not resolve that ambiguity. A signature that replicates in 27/27
settings is a robust signature of an unsigned response. Its consistency
across backbones and seeds raises confidence that the response is a
property of the representation rather than of one dictionary. It does not
supply a sign. Activity matching, matching each specialist to a
non-specialist with nearly identical clean firing and mean activation
(mean firing $0.374$ vs. $0.374$; Appendix A), likewise equates baseline
activity without supplying a direction. "Specialist-like" therefore names a
perturbation response, not a physiological detector. These considerations
do not rule out structured spatial–spectral features. They describe the
limit on what an unsigned, perturbation-defined signature can say on its
own.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder is an operational protocol for grading claims, not a universal
feature finder. Table 1 is the intended reading. A robust
alpha-over-sham signature supports a sensitivity description at Stage 3.
Task relevance requires Stage 4. Physiological naming requires evidence
that the ladder as stated does not itself provide. We do not claim that no
SAE latent is interpretable. We claim only that the vocabulary used to
describe latents should track the evidence actually gathered. A positive
control on another physiological axis would test how the hierarchy behaves
when a label is well-founded. We leave that to a longer version.

Several features of the broader literature motivate this framing. SAE work
in language models has developed automated labeling pipelines in which a
feature's name is derived from its top-activating contexts and then scored
for predictive accuracy (Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2023).
Biosignal models lack an equivalent readable context. Perturbation
summaries are the most accessible substitute, which makes their
interpretive limits correspondingly important. EEG explainability methods
face a parallel issue. Saliency on spectral bands indicates influence on an
output, not the content of an internal unit (Schirrmeister et al., 2017).
The ladder places both kinds of evidence on a common scale.

Limits: remaining settings use one SAE seed; readout groups are unmatched
on baseline activity; $|\Delta f|$ can include TopK rank displacement;
relevance is defined for a logistic probe on mean-pooled codes;
task-readout products cover 21/27 settings (REVE MA/Speech exports were
unavailable); band-stop filtering cannot isolate a biological oscillator,
and a single width-matched sham controls only for the generic effects of
filtering. Conclusions concern descriptions of fitted SAE latents, not
clinical validity or neural causality.

## 5 Conclusion

A $7.3\times$ alpha-over-sham SAE response appears in every setting we
studied, across EEG-native and vision-pretrained backbones and across
depth. It is a robust perturbation signature. It is also unsigned and
defined entirely by an intervention. It therefore supports a description of
sensitivity, not by itself a physiological identity or a role in any
particular readout. Semantic names for SAE features should be justified by
the stage of evidence in Table 1, not by a perturbation response alone.

This study reanalyzes publicly available EEG datasets, recruits no
participants, and makes no clinical predictions; consent and ethics
procedures are inherited from the original releases.

## Appendix C Depth-dependent channel-dropout robustness

Channel dropout progressively destabilizes sparse codes with model depth.
Across all nine model–dataset combinations, late-layer active-set overlap
is lower than early-layer overlap for both random and contiguous dropout
(mean late-minus-early Jaccard $-0.17$ and $-0.20$). The depth effect is
strongest for DINOv3 (contiguous $\Delta$ Jaccard $\approx-0.35$),
intermediate for CBraMod ($\approx-0.19$), and mild for REVE
($\approx-0.07$). Deeper SAE representations are therefore less stable to
spatial perturbation in both EEG-native and cross-modal backbones. Useful
transfer by a vision FM need not bring matching internal robustness. This
architectural observation is secondary to the validation ladder. We report
it here so that it does not compete with the inferential framing in the
main text.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1.

Claims

Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: The abstract and introduction state the empirical scope, and Sections 3–4 distinguish observations from physiological or causal claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

•

The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

•

The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

•

It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

2.

Limitations

Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 4 discusses SAE seeds, TopK competition, baseline-activity differences, linear-probe scope, missing task-analysis settings, and the scope of the sham control.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

•

The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

•

The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

•

The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

•

The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

•

The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

•

If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

•

While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

3.

Theory assumptions and proofs

Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

Answer: [N/A]

Justification: The paper reports empirical analyses and makes no theoretical claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

•

All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

•

All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

•

The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

•

Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

•

Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

4.

Experimental result reproducibility

Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 gives models, data splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, and probe protocol; the supplementary code contains exact configurations.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

•

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

•

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

•

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

(a)

If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

(b)

If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

ANSWER Q1: The paper defines "specialist-like" latents as those in the top quartile of alpha selectivity *and* with channel-dropout fragility at or below the median. Even though alpha is the largest |Δf| band only in 15/27 settings, the paper still finds alpha-sensitive latents because it uses a more stringent definition (selectivity + fragility filter) rather than just raw |Δf| magnitude. This ensures only robust, selective latents are labeled "specialist-like," even if alpha isn’t the dominant band in every case.

---

ANSWER Q2: They should test whether the latents' *clean* activations are positively correlated with trial-wise relative beta power. A passing result would be a mean |r| significantly above zero, with a positive signed correlation (r > 0) in most settings, indicating the latents track beta in unperturbed data.

---

ANSWER Q3: No, it is not a fair comparison. The raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio is sensitive to the amount of spectral energy removed by the notch, which varies across datasets (e.g., 57.2 on BCI vs. 11.8 on Speech). Comparing backbones on different datasets confounds backbone differences with dataset-specific spectral properties.

---

ANSWER Q4: Matching on raw, unstandardized values would match poorly because the distributions of clean firing rate and mean activation likely differ between specialists and candidates. Standardizing on the union of both groups ensures both features are on the same scale, allowing fair comparisons of relative proximity.

---

ANSWER Q5: The mean |r| with relative alpha power would likely *decrease* or remain near zero. The fragility filter excludes latents that are overly sensitive to noise or irrelevant features, which may correlate spuriously with alpha. Without this filter, top-quartile alpha selectivity could include non-specific, noisy latents with misleading correlations.

---

ANSWER Q6: **Not settled**. Appendix B shows raw alpha/sham Jaccard and |Δf| ratios, but it does not directly compare the *sham* notch’s effect on SAE codes to a baseline (e.g., no perturbation). The paper’s main text suggests the sham notch still disrupts codes (e.g., Table 2’s spectral-normalized ratio of 0.28), implying the sham is not entirely neutral.

---
ANSWER Q7: **No**, differences among DINOv3’s settings would not cleanly reflect dataset differences because DINOv3’s token support is limited, requiring reduced expansion (4× or 8×) on some datasets. This architectural constraint could introduce dataset-specific artifacts, confounding dataset effects with model capacity differences.

---
ANSWER Q8: **Speech** settings are most likely among the 10/27 where the time-normalized ratio is ≤1. Speech’s alpha notch removes the least spectral energy (11.8 vs. 57.2 for BCI), so its raw |Δf| advantage (7.3×) collapses more under time-domain normalization, making it more likely to fall below 1.

---
ANSWER Q9: **No**, it would not be a fair test. Specialists and fragile latents differ in their *activity profiles*: specialists fire less in clean data (mean |r| = −0.073) and are less active overall, while fragile latents fire more. Comparing exemplars from these groups could reflect activity differences rather than alpha tracking per se.

---
ANSWER Q10: They should expect a ratio **well below 1** after spectral-energy normalization. The paper shows that even the raw 7.3× advantage collapses to 0.28× when normalized by the energy removed, and this holds across all 27 settings.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense model activations into discrete
latents, which makes individual features easy to inspect and easy to name.
For EEG foundation models, this raises a practical question that precedes
any naming: under which conditions are the fitted latents stable enough,
and reported carefully enough, to be worth interpreting at all? We study
TopK SAEs across 27 settings spanning three backbones (two EEG-pretrained
models and one vision foundation model), three public EEG datasets, and
three network depths. All 27 dictionaries reconstruct held-out activations
well (fraction of variance unexplained between 0.059 and 0.228 at
$L_{0}=32$ ). Paired spatial and spectral perturbations, however, reveal
that sparse codes become progressively less stable with depth: late-layer
active-set overlap under channel dropout is lower than early-layer overlap
in all nine backbone–dataset combinations, most strongly for the vision
backbone. We organize these measurements into a validation ladder for SAE
analyses of biosignal models: reconstruction fidelity, perturbation
stability of the code, consistency across seeds and settings, and
descriptive response profiles under band-limited interventions. The ladder
does not certify that a latent has a particular meaning; it specifies what
should be measured and reported before semantic interpretation is
attempted, and it makes clear that reconstruction quality alone does not
imply a stable or interpretable code.

## 1 Introduction

Foundation models (FMs) for brain and body signals increasingly raise a
mechanistic question: what, exactly, do the learned representations encode?
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) make that question unusually tempting. By
decomposing dense activations into discrete latents, they invite
human-readable names for individual units (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023).
Discreteness, however, is not semantic identifiability. A dictionary can
reconstruct its inputs well while assigning codes that shift substantially
under small, plausible changes to the recording, and a latent whose
behavior depends on which channels happen to be present is a poor
candidate for a physiological label regardless of how its activations
look on a handful of exemplars.

EEG makes these concerns concrete. Recordings vary in montage, channel
count, and noise; electrodes drop out; spectral content differs across
subjects, tasks, and sessions. An SAE fitted to a frozen backbone inherits
all of this variability, and any interpretive claim about its latents is
implicitly a claim that the latent behaves consistently across it. In
language models, SAE interpretability work typically asks whether
features are sparse, reconstructive, monosemantic, or causally
editable (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Marks et al., 2025).
EEG explainability typically asks which input structure influences a
prediction (Schirrmeister et al., 2017). Between these traditions sits a
more basic question for biosignal FMs: how should an SAE analysis of an
EEG backbone be evaluated and reported so that later interpretation rests
on stable ground?

We approach that question empirically across 27 settings spanning frozen
CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and
DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) at early, middle, and late depth on three
public EEG tasks. We include DINOv3 to ask whether the behavior of SAE
codes is peculiar to EEG-pretrained representations or persists when EEG
is encoded through a foundation model pretrained in another modality. In
each setting we train a TopK SAE, pair every clean test trial with
spatially and spectrally perturbed copies, and record how the sparse code
changes. We also fit linear probes on pooled codes to relate the
dictionaries to downstream tasks.

The organizing device is a validation ladder
(Figure 1; Table 1). Its lower rungs are
properties that every SAE analysis can and should report: whether the
dictionary reconstructs held-out activations, whether its codes are stable
under perturbations that should not change the underlying signal content
much, and whether those stability properties are consistent across seeds
and settings. Its upper rung is a descriptive response profile under
band-limited interventions, which characterizes how latents react to
specific spectral changes. Each rung licenses a modest, explicitly scoped
statement; none of them, alone or together, establishes a causal neural
mechanism.

The novelty is not any individual diagnostic. Reconstruction error,
perturbation stability, seed variability, and band-wise response profiles
are ordinary measurements. What we contribute is (i) an operational
hierarchy for reporting SAE analyses of biosignal foundation models, with
each level tied to the scope of claim it supports; (ii) a 27-setting study
showing that SAE reconstruction quality is uniformly good while code
stability degrades systematically with depth; and (iii) a cross-modal
comparison indicating that a vision FM that transfers usefully to EEG need
not bring matching internal robustness to spatial perturbation.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.

We compare EEG-pretrained CBraMod and REVE with DINOv3 ViT-B/16, which
receives channel-by-time EEG images (prefix tokens excluded). Three public
classification sets are sampled at 200 Hz: BCI Competition IV
2a (Tangermann et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2008) (BCI; motor imagery, 22
channels), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (Zyma et al., 2019; Goldberger et al., 2000)
(MA; workload, 20 channels), and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 imagined
speech (Jeong et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020) (Speech; 64 channels).
Splits are fixed; backbones are frozen. We refer to each combination of
backbone, dataset, and depth as a setting, giving 27 settings in
total. The datasets were chosen to cover distinct paradigms, channel
counts, and signal-to-noise regimes, so that conclusions about code
stability are not tied to a single montage or task. Licenses and compute
are listed in Appendix F.

#### TopK SAEs.

For $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

We set $k=32$ and train with reconstruction MSE plus AuxK dead-latent
recovery (Gao et al., 2025). Token activations from early, middle, or late
blocks are layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$ before mixing.
Dictionary expansion is $16\times$ except where token support motivates
$4\times$ or $8\times$ for DINOv3, giving 27 dictionaries. All converge to
test FVU in $[0.059,0.228]$ with $L_{0}=32$ . The BCI middle setting of each
backbone is retrained under three seeds. Further training details are in
Appendix A. The TopK formulation fixes sparsity exactly, which removes one
common source of variation between dictionaries and makes stability
comparisons across settings more direct than with an $\ell_{1}$ penalty
whose effective sparsity drifts during training.

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

Each clean test trial is paired with a perturbed copy. Spatial
interventions zero random channels or contiguous windows. Spectral
interventions apply a fourth-order zero-phase Butterworth band-stop at
$\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ , or high- $\gamma$ , plus an 8–12 Hz
alpha test against a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham. SAEs stay frozen. We
record sparse-code cosine, active-set Jaccard, and $|\Delta f_{j}|$ . All
perturbations are applied to the raw signal before the backbone, so the
same clean trial serves as its own reference and differences in code
reflect only the intervention. We also record the time-domain magnitude
$\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}/\|x\|_{2}$ of every perturbation so that responses can
be placed alongside the size of the input change that produced them.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

Selectivity is
$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b^{\prime}\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b^{\prime}}|$ ,
a descriptive summary of how much more latent $j$ moves under band $b$
than under the other five bands. Channel-dropout fragility is the
analogous quantity for spatial interventions. Mean-pooled SAE codes feed
logistic probes on the fixed split. Importance is
$|w_{j}|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_{j}]$ . A group ablation sets the codes of
a selected set of latents to zero and measures the resulting change in
probe balanced accuracy, with groups matched in size. In the frozen-probe
variant the probe is trained on clean codes and the ablation is applied
only at test time; in the retrained variant the probe is refit after
ablation. For clean-data inspection we compute each latent’s activation
across unperturbed test trials and the trial-wise Welch spectrum, so that
perturbation-derived summaries can be read alongside the latent’s ordinary
behavior.

Confidence intervals in the text are percentile 95% intervals from 10,000
bootstrap resamples of settings (27 settings, or 21 for task analyses), not
of individual latents.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

The first rung of the ladder is passed everywhere: all 27 dictionaries
reach test FVU between 0.059 and 0.228 at $L_{0}=32$ , with no backbone or
dataset standing out as poorly reconstructed. Reconstruction, however, says
nothing about how codes behave when the input changes. Spectral band-stops,
including the alpha notch, alter sparse codes in every backbone, but these
responses sit within a broader pattern of code instability that is most
visible under spatial perturbation and grows with depth. We therefore
treat individual spectral responses as one component of a code’s general
sensitivity to input change rather than as an isolated signature, and
place them alongside the magnitude of the corresponding input change
before reading them further.

Channel-dropout robustness decreases with depth across all nine
backbone–dataset combinations (Table 2). The effect is strongest for
DINOv3, intermediate for CBraMod, and mild for REVE. Deeper SAE codes are
thus less stable under the kind of perturbation that routinely occurs in
practice when electrodes are noisy or missing, and this holds for both
EEG-native and cross-modal backbones. A stability statement made at one
depth therefore does not transfer automatically to another, and any later
interpretive claim must be indexed by the layer at which it was made. The
cross-modal contrast is also informative: DINOv3 can encode EEG images
usefully for downstream probes, yet its deeper sparse codes are the least
robust to spatial perturbation, so transfer performance and internal
robustness should be reported as separate properties.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe balanced accuracy spans 0.236–0.625 across the 21 settings with
task-analysis codes, so ablations are compared within settings rather
than across them. Selectivity and importance answer different questions.
Selectivity summarizes how a latent’s firing changes when a particular
band is removed from the input; importance summarizes how much a fitted
linear readout weights that latent on clean data. A latent can be strongly
affected by a band-stop and receive little weight from a probe, or the
reverse, and nothing in the construction of either quantity forces them
to agree. We therefore report them as separate columns of the analysis
rather than using one as a proxy for the other.

The group-ablation protocol is designed accordingly. Zeroing a size-matched
group of latents and measuring the change in balanced accuracy, with the
probe either frozen or retrained, tests whether a readout depends on that
group; it does not test what the group encodes. Effects shrink after
probe retraining, as expected when the readout can redistribute weight to
correlated latents, and the ordering of groups on the BCI middle setting
depends on the SAE seed. Groups chosen by perturbation criteria also
differ in baseline activity, which complicates direct comparison. For
these reasons the ablation results are presented descriptively in
Appendix D, and we draw no conclusion about task relevance from them.
Relevance in any case is defined here only for a logistic probe on
mean-pooled codes and does not speak to nonlinear or fine-tuned behavior.

### 3.3 Independent observational validation fails in the intended direction

Clean signals provide a check that no perturbation can supply on its own:
a latent described in terms of a spectral band should also be describable
in terms of how it behaves on ordinary, unmodified recordings. We
therefore inspected, for each setting, the clean test trials on which
selected latents fire most strongly, together with their Welch spectra
(Appendix A). This inspection did not yield a consistent band-specific
picture that would support assigning spectral names to the latents, and
the exemplar view proved sensitive to which latents were selected and to
their baseline firing rates. High-baseline latents dominate any
exemplar-based summary simply because they are active on more trials.

We take two lessons from this for the ladder. First, observational checks
on clean data should use quantities that were not involved in choosing
the latents, and should condition on baseline activity, for example by
comparing against controls matched in firing rate and mean activation
(Appendix E). Second, top-activating exemplars are a useful qualitative
aid but a weak basis for a label, because they condition on the extreme
of the activation distribution. These checks do not rule out structured
spatial–spectral features; they indicate only that the present analysis
does not reach the rung at which a simple frequency-band reading could be
asserted, and the descriptive response profiles should be read with that
in mind.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder is an operational reporting protocol, not a universal feature
finder. Table 1 is the intended reading: each rung adds a
measurement and licenses a correspondingly scoped statement. Our results
populate the lower rungs. Reconstruction is uniformly good, which is
necessary but uninformative about code behavior; stability under spatial
perturbation degrades with depth across every backbone–dataset
combination; and spectral responses are best read as part of a code’s
overall sensitivity to input change. Semantic interpretation of
individual latents lies above the rungs we test, and we do not claim that
any latent studied here has, or lacks, a particular physiological meaning.

The depth trend has practical consequences for EEG work. Electrode
dropout and noisy channels are common in real recordings, so a latent
whose activity depends on the exact channel set is fragile in exactly the
way that matters for deployment. That the effect is strongest for the
vision backbone suggests that cross-modal transfer, however effective for
downstream accuracy, should be accompanied by explicit robustness
reporting. More broadly, the same SAE analysis applied to different layers
of the same model can support quite different stability statements, so
layer choice should be reported as a primary experimental variable rather
than an implementation detail. A positive control on another physiological
axis, where ground truth is better constrained, would test how far up the
ladder a well-behaved dictionary can climb; we leave that to a longer
version.

Limits: remaining settings use one SAE seed; groups compared in ablations
are unmatched on baseline activity; $|\Delta f|$ can include TopK rank
displacement; relevance is defined for a logistic probe on mean-pooled
codes; task-readout products cover 21/27 settings (REVE MA/Speech exports
were unavailable); band-stop filtering cannot isolate a biological
oscillator; and clean-data inspection was qualitative. Conclusions concern
the behavior and reporting of fitted SAE latents, not clinical validity or
neural causality.

## 5 Conclusion

Across 27 settings, TopK SAEs on frozen EEG and vision foundation models
reconstruct held-out activations well, but their codes become
progressively less stable under channel dropout as depth increases, most
strongly for the cross-modal backbone. Reconstruction quality therefore
does not imply a stable code, and stability at one layer does not imply
stability at another. Semantic names for SAE features should be preceded
by the measurements in Table 1 and scoped by the rung of
evidence they reach.

#### Ethics statement.

This study reanalyzes publicly available EEG datasets, recruits no
participants, and makes no clinical predictions; consent and ethics
procedures are inherited from the original releases.

## Appendix A Additional experimental details

Layer groups mix consecutive transformer blocks after per-layer $\ell_{2}$
normalization: blocks 0–3 / 4–7 / 8–11 for CBraMod and DINOv3 (12
blocks) and 0–6 / 7–14 / 15–21 for REVE (22 blocks). DINOv3 dictionary
width is reduced to $4\times$ on Mental Arithmetic and $8\times$ on BCI
where token support is limited; all other settings use $16\times$ . Training
uses reconstruction MSE plus AuxK with $k=32$ . Multi-seed analyses retrain
only the BCI middle setting of each backbone.

For clean-data inspection we stream, for a small number of selected
latents per setting, each latent’s top-five clean test activations
together with the corresponding trials. Welch spectra quantify relative
band power on those tails. Because this view conditions on the activation
extreme, it is used qualitatively; correlational summaries over all
trials are the more appropriate primary quantity for any future
observational test.

Activity-matched controls, where used, are taken from the same
dictionary. For each selected latent we choose the unused non-selected
latent minimizing squared $z$ -distance in clean firing rate and mean
activation (features standardized on the union of selected latents and
the candidate pool), sampling without replacement.

## Appendix C Depth-dependent channel-dropout robustness

Channel dropout progressively destabilizes sparse codes with model depth.
Across all nine model–dataset combinations, late-layer active-set overlap
is lower than early-layer overlap for both random and contiguous dropout
(mean late-minus-early Jaccard $-0.17$ and $-0.20$ ). The depth effect is
strongest for DINOv3 (contiguous $\Delta$ Jaccard $\approx-0.35$ ),
intermediate for CBraMod ( $\approx-0.19$ ), and mild for REVE
( $\approx-0.07$ ). Deeper SAE representations are therefore less stable to
spatial perturbation in both EEG-native and cross-modal backbones: useful
transfer by a vision FM need not bring matching internal robustness.
Contiguous dropout, which removes spatially adjacent channels, is
consistently more damaging than random dropout of the same number of
channels, consistent with representations that pool information over
local scalp neighborhoods. This observation is summarized in the main text
(Table 2) because it is the clearest stability result across the
27 settings.

## NeurIPS Paper Checklist

1.

Claims

Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: The abstract and introduction state the empirical scope, and Sections 3–4 distinguish measured stability properties from physiological or causal claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

•

The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

•

The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

•

It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

2.

Limitations

Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 4 discusses SAE seeds, TopK competition, baseline-activity differences, linear-probe scope, missing task-analysis settings, qualitative clean-data inspection, and dataset scope.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

•

The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

•

The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

•

The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

•

The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

•

The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

•

If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

•

While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

3.

Theory assumptions and proofs

Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

Answer: [N/A]

Justification: The paper reports empirical analyses and makes no theoretical claims.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

•

All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

•

All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

•

The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

•

Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

•

Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

4.

Experimental result reproducibility

Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 gives models, data splits, preprocessing, SAE construction, perturbations, metrics, and probe protocol; the supplementary code contains exact configurations.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

•

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

•

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

•

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

(a)

If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

(b)

If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

(c)

If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

(d)

We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

5.

Open access to data and code

Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Datasets and backbone implementations are public and cited. An anonymized code archive with training and analysis scripts is provided as supplementary material; checkpoints and raw EEG are omitted because of size.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

•

Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

•

The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

•

The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

•

The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

•

At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

•

Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

6.

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Section 2 reports the split policy, preprocessing, SAE sparsity and expansion, perturbation bands, metrics, and classifier protocol; full training details are in the supplement.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

•

The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

7.

Experiment statistical significance

Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

Answer: [Yes]

Justification: Intervals for setting-level summaries are percentile 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27 settings, or 21 for task analyses), as described in Section 2 and Appendix E. The resampling unit is the setting, not the latent. Initialization variability is additionally examined for the BCI middle-layer setting under three SAE seeds.

Guidelines:

•

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

•

The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

•

The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

•

The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

•

The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

•

It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

•

It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

•

For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

•

If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

8.

Experiments compute resources

Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

Justification: Appendix F reports NVIDIA A100 GPUs on a shared academic Slurm cluster and an estimate of about 300 GPU-hours for the reported pipeline, excluding unused exploratory runs.

The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

Code of ethics

Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

Justification: The study reanalyzes public research datasets, reports limitations, and makes no clinical or individual-level claims.

The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

Broader impacts

Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

Justification: Section 4 motivates more careful validation and reporting of biosignal interpretations and limits the findings to representation auditing rather than clinical or neural causality.

Guidelines:

•

If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. That would support a representational label; a task-relevant label would additionally require readout intervention to change task behavior.

ANSWER Q9: Selection uses the absolute firing change under an artificial notch, which can capture generic distortion sensitivity, TopK rank displacement, or responses to removing background spectral energy rather than encoding alpha abundance. Consequently, such latents can be anti-correlated with alpha power on unperturbed trials.

ANSWER Q10: They should correlate each latent’s activation on clean trials with an independently measured trial-wise relative beta power, preferably using activity-matched controls. Passing would require reproducible covariance in the expected positive direction, beyond what comparable non-specialists show.

ANSWER Q11: It would tend to exclude that latent. A feature dependent on a small channel cluster should be fragile to channel dropout, whereas specialist-like latents are required to have channel-dropout fragility at or below the median.

ANSWER Q12: Contradicted. Perturbation sensitivity is the ladder’s first evidential rung and supports the limited claim that a latent is alpha-sensitive; the paper argues that it is insufficient by itself for an alpha-representing label.

ANSWER Q13: Removed-spectral-energy normalization is the more conservative screen. It reduced the pooled ratio to 0.28 with 0/27 settings above one, whereas time-domain normalization left a ratio of 1.32 and 17/27 settings above one.

ANSWER Q14: Active-set overlap is a bounded, discrete measure that records which TopK latents change membership but ignores how much their firing magnitudes move. This compresses differences between alpha and sham responses relative to the continuous \(|\Delta f|\) metric.

ANSWER Q15: The alpha notch removes tens of times more spectral energy than the sham—11.8 to 57.2 times depending on the dataset. Dividing a raw ratio near 7.33 by an effective energy imbalance of roughly 26 gives \(7.33/26\approx0.28\).

ANSWER Q16: Time-domain relative \(L_2\) distortion scales approximately with the square root of removed energy, so it applies a much smaller correction than direct spectral-energy normalization. ANSWER Q17: Firing rate and mean activation have very different numerical scales and variances, so raw squared distance would be dominated by the larger-scale feature, likely firing rate. Z-standardization gives both features comparable influence on the match.

ANSWER Q21: Speech. Its alpha/sham removed-energy ratio is 11.8, compared with 34.6 for MA and 57.2 for BCI, so its raw comparison is least inflated by unequal amounts of removed signal.

ANSWER Q1: Yes. Using Appendix B, the disruption ratios are approximately 2.54 for CBraMod, 3.36 for REVE, and 2.37 for DINOv3, whose average is about 2.75—close to the reported 2.77.

ANSWER Q2: Importance is defined as \(|w_j|\mathbb{E}[c_j]\), not just \(|w_j|\). A latent with a large probe weight can therefore have low importance if it fires rarely or has low mean activation.

ANSWER Q3: Spectral normalization approximately divides each raw response ratio by the alpha/sham removed-energy ratio, which ranges from 11.8 to 57.2. Applying those denominators to 7.33 gives dataset-level values of roughly 0.13, 0.21, and 0.62, averaging about 0.32; differences in setting-level raw ratios can readily yield the reported 0.28.

ANSWER Q4: The 15/27 result concerns which band has the largest aggregate response in a setting, whereas “specialist-like” is a relative latent-level selection based on the top quartile of alpha selectivity plus low channel-dropout fragility. Alpha need not dominate the whole setting for some individual latents to satisfy those criteria.

ANSWER Q5: DINOv3 has a much larger sham response than REVE: \(0.00033\) versus \(0.00014\). Indeed, DINOv3’s absolute alpha response is larger than REVE’s, so its lower ratio is caused by the larger denominator.

ANSWER Q6: The positive-control latent should respond to the target perturbation, survive distortion normalization and competing-perturbation controls, and independently covary in the expected direction with that physiology in clean data. A task-relevant label would additionally require readout intervention to change task behavior.

ANSWER Q7: Supported. DINOv3 has the lowest sham-notch Jaccard, 0.782 versus 0.819 for CBraMod and 0.841 for REVE, indicating the greatest average active-set disruption under the sham notch.

ANSWER Q8: Contradicted. The mean selectivity–importance correlation is weak but positive, \(r=0.107\) with a 95% CI of \([0.068,0.146]\); the paper argues that selectivity is not a strong or reliable marker of importance, not that the relationship is exactly zero.

ANSWER Q9: No. DINOv3 dictionary expansion is confounded with dataset—\(8\times\) for BCI, \(4\times\) for MA, and \(16\times\) for Speech—along with differences in channels, tasks, and spectra, so comparisons would not isolate dataset effects.

ANSWER Q10: Specialists are a subset of the top selectivity quartile, so they comprise at most one quarter of the dictionary. The non-specialist pool is consequently much larger, allowing a distinct nearest match for each specialist without replacement.

ANSWER Q11: A ratio measures alpha response relative to sham response, not absolute alpha response. REVE’s ratio is largest mainly because its sham response is especially small; its alpha \(|\Delta f|\), \(0.00127\), is lower than those of both CBraMod and DINOv3.

ANSWER Q12: They should expect spectral-energy normalization to reduce the ratio substantially, plausibly below one, because the alpha notch removes much more energy than the sham notch. The paper’s 27 settings all behaved this way, although it cannot guarantee the outcome for a new architecture.

ANSWER Q13: It would tend to exclude that latent if dependence on a small channel cluster makes it fragile to channel dropout, because specialists must have at-or-below-median dropout fragility. It could remain if the measured dropout interventions rarely hit the cluster or the code remains robust, so exclusion is not guaranteed.

ANSWER Q14: Appendix B reports ratios formed from backbone-level averaged \(|\Delta f|\) values, while the pooled statistic can average setting-level ratios; a ratio of averages need not equal an average of ratios. Rounding of the displayed backbone values can also contribute.

ANSWER Q15: Not fully. Fragile latents have substantially different baseline activity—reported as firing \(8.9\times\) more—so conditioning on each group’s top five activations can compare different activation regimes; this is why the unconditioned all-trial correlation is primary and activity-matched non-specialists are also used.

ANSWER Q16: Firing rate and mean activation have different numerical scales and variances. With raw squared distance, the higher-scale or higher-variance feature would dominate the matching objective, potentially leaving the other feature poorly matched; z-scoring gives them comparable influence.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. REVE’s MA and Speech task-analysis exports were unavailable, so the task-code selectivity–importance analysis covers REVE on BCI rather than all three datasets.

ANSWER Q18: Selection uses the magnitude of the change under an artificial band-stop, which can reflect removed energy, broad input distortion, TopK rank displacement, or an inverse response rather than positive alpha encoding. Because \(|\Delta f|\) also discards direction, such selection does not imply positive covariance with alpha power in clean EEG.

ANSWER Q19: No. A single-seed \(r=0.3\) is only a setting-specific association and is within the range observed in the paper; the team should assess seed stability, uncertainty, activity confounds, and preferably direct ablation before claiming readout importance.

ANSWER Q20: It can overstate usefulness when the latent is highly active and heavily weighted but has little class-conditional contrast, or when correlated latents provide redundant information. The score is not a marginal causal contribution and does not measure how much accuracy falls when that latent is removed.

ANSWER Q21: Contradicted. REVE’s late group covers blocks 15–21, whereas CBraMod’s covers blocks 8–11, so REVE’s late group is neither at lower absolute block indices nor composed of fewer blocks; architecture-specific factors could explain the difference, but this proposed explanation cannot.

ANSWER Q22: Contradicted. By alpha Jaccard, REVE is more disrupted than DINOv3 but CBraMod is less disrupted; by absolute alpha \(|\Delta f|\), CBraMod exceeds DINOv3 while REVE does not. Appendix B therefore does not support a common EEG-pretrained-versus-vision-pretrained ordering.

ANSWER Q1: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

The paper does not show that the selectivity-importance decoupling holds for REVE on all three datasets. In fact, the table shows that the selectivity-importance correlation is only $|r|=0.143$ for specialists in the REVE task, which is higher than the $|r|=-0.073$ for specialists in the BCI task. This suggests that the decoupling might not hold across different datasets.

ANSWER Q2: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

A pooled spectral-normalized ratio of 0.28 is roughly what one would expect if every setting simply had a raw ratio near the pooled 7.33 because the spectral-energy normalization is designed to remove the alpha notch, and the raw ratio is highly sensitive to this notch. The normalization process is intended to make the raw ratio more comparable across settings.

ANSWER Q3: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

The paper does not show that the three backbones rank the same on how much alpha removal disrupts SAE codes relative to the sham. In fact, the table shows that the raw |Δf| ratio is largest for CBraMod, followed by REVE, and then DINOv3. This suggests that the disruption of SAE codes by alpha removal might vary across backbones.

ANSWER Q4: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

The setting-level 95% CI for the raw alpha/sham ratio, [6.18, 8.68], would be a reliable range for the raw ratio of a new backbone because the CI is relatively narrow, indicating that the true ratio is likely to be close to the mean value of 7.33.

ANSWER Q5: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

According to Appendix B, DINOv3's raw alpha/sham |Δf| ratio (5.1) is lower than REVE's (8.9) because DINOv3 has fewer absolute blocks than REVE, which may result in a smaller disruption of SAE codes by alpha removal.

ANSWER Q6: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

Every setting nonetheless contains alpha 'specialist-like' latents because the paper defines specialists as having a top-quartile alpha selectivity, which is a relatively high threshold. This means that even if the raw |Δf| ratio is not extremely large, a latent can still be considered specialist-like if its selectivity is above this threshold.

ANSWER Q7: Answer supported, contradicted, or not settled, and why.

# When Is an SAE Feature Interpretable?

A Validation Ladder for EEG Foundation Models

Yucong Cao

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Chenqi Li

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Tingting Zhu

Affiliation: Department of Engineering Science

Affiliation: University of Oxford

###### Abstract

Across 27 settings (three backbones, three EEG datasets, three depths), an
8–12 Hz band-stop changes SAE latent firing $7.3\times$ more than an
equal-width sham notch (95% CI $[6.2,8.7]$, bootstrapped over settings).
Per unit removed spectral energy the ratio is $0.28\times$ (95% CI
$[0.22,0.36]$), exceeding one in none of the 27 settings. Latents selected
on alpha-removal response have mean $r=-0.073$ with clean-EEG relative
alpha power. We give a validation ladder for semantic readings of SAE
latents—response, distortion-controlled response, specificity against broad
fragility, and clean-data correspondence—with task-classifier relevance as a
separate branch.

## 1 Introduction

SAEs decompose dense foundation-model (FM) activations into discrete latents
amenable to naming (Gao et al., 2025; Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023).
We audit “alpha feature” labels on frozen
CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025), REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025), and
DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) at early, middle, and late depth on three
public EEG tasks. Raw alpha-over-sham firing change is $7.3\times$ in
every one of 27 settings; per unit removed spectral energy it is
$0.28\times$, exceeding one in $0/27$. Latents are chosen by perturbation
response and evaluated on clean signals; the selected units fire when
relative alpha power is lower, not higher.

The ladder (Figure 1; Table 1): Stages 1–3 (sensitivity, distortion-controlled
selectivity, specificity) and Stage 5 (independent observational validation)
yield a representational claim; Stage 4 (readout intervention) is a side
branch, required only for functional relevance to a specified readout.

The individual diagnostics—sensitivity, specificity, intervention,
downstream relevance, external validation—are standard. The contribution is
the identification of a recurrent inferential failure in SAE-based
biosignal interpretation and an operational hierarchy of alternatives to
exclude before physiological labelling. SAE interpretability in language
models targets sparsity, reconstruction, monosemanticity, or causal
editability (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Marks et al., 2025);
EEG explainability targets input attribution (Schirrmeister et al., 2017).
Our question: when does a perturbation-responsive SAE latent warrant a
physiological label?

DINOv3 tests persistence under a foundation model pretrained in another
modality. Contributions: (i) a forked validation protocol supporting claims
at graded strength; (ii) a 27-setting demonstration that a $7.3\times$
alpha-sensitive signature is largely an input-distortion artifact; (iii)
specialist-like latents neither track clean-EEG alpha in the intended
direction nor are preferentially important to a linear readout.

Table 1: Evidence available after each stage, and the claim that evidence
supports. None of these establish a causal neural mechanism.

## 2 Experimental design

#### Backbones and data.

CBraMod, REVE, and DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (channel-by-time EEG images, prefix
tokens excluded) on three 200 Hz sets: BCI Competition IV
2a (Tangermann et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2008) (BCI; motor imagery, 22
channels), PhysioNet Mental Arithmetic (Zyma et al., 2019; Goldberger et al., 2000)
(MA; workload, 20 channels), and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 imagined
speech (Jeong et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020) (Speech; 64 channels).
Fixed splits, frozen backbones; backbone × dataset × depth gives 27
settings. Licenses and compute: Appendix F.

#### TopK SAEs.

For $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

| | $c=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{k}\left((x-b_{\rm dec})W_{\rm enc}+b_{\rm enc}\right)\right),\qquad\hat{x}=cW_{\rm dec}+b_{\rm dec}.$
|

$k=32$; loss MSE + AuxK (Gao et al., 2025). Early/middle/late block tokens,
layer-normalized to $\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}=\sqrt{d}$ before mixing. Expansion
$16\times$, or $4\times$/$8\times$ for DINOv3 under limited token support;
27 dictionaries, test FVU $[0.059,0.228]$, $L_{0}=32$. BCI middle of each
backbone retrained over three seeds (Appendix A).

#### Perturbations and distortion control.

Clean test trials paired with perturbed copies; SAEs frozen. Spatial: random
channel or contiguous-window zeroing. Spectral: fourth-order zero-phase
Butterworth band-stop at $\delta,\theta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ , high-
$\gamma$ , and 8–12 Hz alpha vs. width-matched 30–34 Hz sham. Recorded:
sparse-code cosine, active-set Jaccard, $|\Delta f_{j}|$. Under the $1/f$
EEG spectrum, alpha/sham removed-energy ratios are 57.2 / 34.6 / 11.8 on
BCI / MA / Speech. Responses are reported raw and divided by
$\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}/\|x\|_{2}$ or by removed spectral-energy fraction.

#### Selectivity, probes, and independent validation.

$s_{j,b}=|\Delta f_{j,b}|-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{b^{\prime}\neq b}|\Delta f_{j,b^{\prime}}|$ ;
specialist-like alpha latents: top-quartile $s_{j,\alpha}$, channel-dropout
fragility $\le$ median. Readout contrasts: size-matched general-fragile and
random groups; clean-alpha contrast: activity-matched non-specialists
(nearest clean firing rate and mean activation, without replacement).
Logistic probes on mean-pooled codes, fixed split; importance
$|w_{j}|\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[c_{j}]$. Group ablation zeroes a size-matched
set (specialist-like, general-fragile, random) and records $\Delta$
balanced accuracy, with the probe frozen (trained on clean codes, ablation
at test) or refit after ablation. Clean activation is correlated with
trial-wise relative alpha power (unused in selection) for 12,041 latents in
each named group.

CIs: percentile 95%, 10,000 bootstrap resamples of settings (27, or 21 for
task analyses), not latents.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 A large raw alpha response collapses under distortion control

Alpha/sham firing change is 5–9 $\times$ per backbone; alpha lowers code
overlap in all 27 settings (Appendix B). In the six-band sweep alpha is the
maximum- $|\Delta f|$ and minimum-Jaccard band in 15/27 settings.
Channel-dropout robustness decreases with depth in all nine
backbone–dataset combinations, most for DINOv3 (Appendix C).

Table 2: Pooled alpha/sham $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings, raw and
normalized; 95% CIs bootstrapped over settings.

| $|\Delta f|$ ratio, 27 settings | Mean | 95% CI | Settings $>1$

| raw | 7.33 | $[6.18,8.68]$ | 27/27

| per unit time-domain distortion | 1.32 | $[1.12,1.55]$ | 17/27

| per unit removed spectral energy | 0.28 | $[0.22,0.36]$ | 0/27

The removed-energy denominator varies almost fivefold across datasets; the
two normalizations bracket the ratio. Code-overlap ratios: raw 2.77, then
0.51 and 0.11.

### 3.2 Alpha selectivity is not readout importance

Probe balanced accuracy 0.236–0.625; ablations compared within setting.
Selectivity–importance Pearson $r=0.107$ (CI $[0.068,0.146]$), 21 settings
(Figure 2A); $|r|\leq 0.32$ in all nine BCI-middle retrainings.

## 4 Discussion and limitations

The ladder excludes specific alternatives; it is not a feature finder. The
claim concerns the $7.3\times$ alpha signature, not SAE latents in general.
A positive control on another physiological axis is deferred to a longer

Limits: one SAE seed outside BCI middle; readout groups unmatched on

task-readout products cover 21/27 settings (REVE MA/Speech exports

The $7.3\times$ alpha-over-sham response, present in every setting, fails
